title: Bayern Munich joins Arsenal in the race for Champions League winner
description: Bayern Munich have joined Arsenal and Liverpool in the race to sign Bradley Barcola this summer, with growing speculation that the French attacker could leave Paris Saint-Germain during the current tr...
fullText:
Bayern Munich have joined Arsenal and Liverpool in the race to sign Bradley Barcola this summer, with growing speculation that the French attacker could leave Paris Saint-Germain during the current transfer window.

Barcola has reportedly informed PSG that he does not intend to sign a new contract at the club and would prefer to continue his career in the Premier League. His situation has attracted interest from several major clubs looking to strengthen their attacking options.

For several months, Arsenal and Liverpool have worked to secure a move for Barcola as they look to add another important attacking player to their squads. Both clubs have identified the Frenchman as a player who could make a significant impact.

However, neither side has managed to make progress in recent weeks because PSG have maintained their position that the player is not available for transfer. Despite that stance, there remains a possibility that the situation could change before the transfer window closes.

According to Fichajes, Bayern Munich have now entered the race for Barcola’s signature as they look to ensure their squad contains the quality required to compete at the highest level.

When Barcola returns from pre-season, he could request that PSG allow him to leave this summer. The attacker is expected to hope that the French champions will reconsider their position and agree to negotiate a potential transfer.

If PSG decide that a sale is possible, Bayern Munich are prepared to compete strongly for his signature and challenge Arsenal and Liverpool for the forward.

The German club’s interest adds further competition to an already difficult pursuit for the Premier League sides. Arsenal and Liverpool will now have to continue monitoring the situation while waiting to see whether PSG change their stance on Barcola’s future.

With several top European clubs interested, the coming weeks could be crucial in determining where the Frenchman plays next season. If he does become available, a major transfer battle could develop between some of Europe’s leading clubs.

title: What did Yankees get for Camilo Doval? Pirates send two prospects for veteran reliever
description: The Yankees are getting two intriguing prospects for Camilo Doval.
fullText:
What did Yankees get for Camilo Doval? Pirates send two prospects for veteran reliever originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The New York Yankees made their first move of the 2026 MLB trade deadline. But it wasn't an acquisition to bolster their World Series odds.

Instead, according to ESPN's Jeff Passan, the Yankees sent Camilo Doval to the Pittsburgh Pirates. But what did the Yankees get for Doval? Passan reported that two prospects are coming over in the deal, but which prospects did the Yankees get?

According to Francys Romero of Beisbolfr.com, the Yankees are picking up Luis Cruz and Omar Alfonzo in exchange for Doval.

"The New York Yankees are acquiring minor leaguers Omar Alfonzo and Luis Cruz from the Pirates' Dominican Summer League affiliate in exchange for Camilo Doval, per sources," Romero reports.

While the Yankees aren't getting one of the Pirates' top prospects for Doval, these two youngsters are fairly interesting additions.

Alfonzo is a 22-year-old catcher prospect who has a .238 batting average and a .756 OPS this season in 62 games for the Pirates. He is the Pirates' No. 17-ranked prospect according to MLB Pipeline.

Cruz, on the other hand, is an 18-year-old outfield prospect who is unranked in the Pirates farm system. He has a .300 batting average and an .843 OPS in 50 at-bats this season, and is just getting started with his professional career.

MORE: Yankees linked to Padres for potential rotation for bullpen swap

To land both of those prospects, the Yankees sent Doval to the Pirates. The former All-Star reliever, whom the Yankees acquired at last year's trade deadline, has a 4.54 ERA and -0.8 bWAR this season for New York.

He's under club control through 2027, but the Yankees have parted ways amid his struggles since coming to the team in a trade with the San Francisco Giants.

In exchange for Doval, the Pirates are sending Alfonzo and Cruz to the Yankees. It's an intriguing return for the Yankees, as they upgrade their catching depth, and pick up a teenage outfield prospect who could rise the farm system rankings in the coming years.

fullText:
Former Eastern Michigan player Sisi Eleko plans to transfer in light of the Colorado ruling, her representative at Next Page NIL told On3.

Eleko’s decision to return for one more season of collegiate basketball comes after Judge Charlotte Sweeney of the U.S. District Court of Colorado granted a class-wide preliminary injunction that requires the NCAA to declare eligible all high school class of 2022 athletes who exhausted four seasons of eligibility this spring.

Eleko spent her first two seasons (2022-24) at Canisius before transferring to Eastern Michigan for the last two seasons. Last year, the 6-2 forward averaged 17.6 points and 9.9 rebounds per game.

“All persons in the United States who began to play in collegiate sports in the 2022-2023 season, competed in NCAA Division I sports, and completed four years of eligibility as defined by the NCAA’s prior rules by the conclusion of the 2025-2026 season, and are therefore barred from playing a fifth season due to the NCAA’s adoption and immediate implementation of the Five-Year Eligibility Rule,” the class certification read.

title: Red Sox get trade odds update from ESPN about Angels shortstop trade target
description: These trade odds aren't too terrible for Boston.
fullText:
Red Sox get trade odds update from ESPN about Angels shortstop trade target originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The Boston Red Sox are on the hunt for more infield help as the 2026 MLB trade deadline approaches. They've had their eyes on a ton of different options, but there are a few that are more appealing than the rest.

While there has been a link to some second baseman this summer, the real need for the Red Sox comes at shortstop. Trevor Story isn't someone the Red Sox can trust, so adding a top-tier shortstop via trade would make sense.

One of their top targets is the Los Angeles Angels' 25-year-old star, Zach Neto. Two days until the trade deadline, ESPN's Jeff Passan and Kiley McDaniel shared the updated odds of the Angels trading Neto, and for the Red Sox, they aren't too bad.

"Zach Neto, SS, Los Angeles Angels. Chance of being traded: 40%," Passan and McDaniel write. "... Best fits: Red Sox, Braves, Blue Jays, Twins, Yankees."

While this 40% trade projection from Passan and McDaniel doesn't mean there's a 40% chance the Red Sox acquire the young infielder, it does mean that those are the odds the Angels actually trade him.

There's less than a coin-flip odds of Neto being traded, but a 40% chance that Neto is dealt is still a bit higher than some of the other trade targets around baseball.

Mason Miller is at 20%, and Jeremy Pena, the Houston Astros shortstop the Red Sox have been linked to this year, has just a 25% chance of being traded.

MORE: Red Sox predicted to trade for Tigers’ Gleyber Torres at deadline

Neto, the 25-year-old shortstop who is under club control through the 2029 season and has a .232 batting average with 19 home runs and 2.7 bWAR this season across 422 at-bats, would be one of the best options for Boston amid their infield need.

The Red Sox still would have to compete with some of the other teams around baseball, with the Atlanta Braves and New York Yankees being two clubs that could also pursue Neto this summer.

But, if nothing else, hearing that there is a 40% chance that the Angels trade Neto should open the door for the Red Sox to have a fighting chance to land maybe the best possible shortstop upgrade they could have this summer.

title: Victor Wembanyama's unselfish choice has Dylan Harper calling him 'the most genuine person ever'
description: Dylan Harper shares why Victor Wembanyama's selfless contract decision continues to inspire the Spurs' young core.
fullText:
Victor Wembanyama's unselfish choice has Dylan Harper calling him 'the most genuine person ever' originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The San Antonio Spurs reached the NBA Finals this past season behind All-NBA center and unanimous Defensive Player of the Year Victor Wembanyama. After witnessing his rapid rise to superstardom, the Spurs wasted no time rewarding him with a massive contract extension.

The deal came at a discount, as Wembanyama was eligible to sign an extension worth more than $300 million. Instead, he accepted a smaller figure to provide San Antonio with greater financial flexibility.

Unsurprisingly, Wembanyama earned widespread praise for the decision. Recently, Spurs rising star Dylan Harper shared his thoughts on Wembanyama and his willingness to take less than the maximum extension.

“I feel like for a 22-year-old, he's probably one of the best leaders I've been around, just the way he carries himself, his maturity, from top to bottom, whether it's basketball treatment, in the weight room, personal life,” Harper said.

“I feel like he's kind of structured his life in a way that has worked for him, and I think he's the most genuine person ever. When that came out, I feel like yes, it was a surprise to everyone. But I mean, that's just the type of person he is.”

Wembanyama explained during NBA 2K27 promotional interviews that his main goal was to preserve cap space and maintain roster flexibility under the NBA's luxury tax aprons. The five-year extension keeps the French superstar under contract with San Antonio through the 2031–32 season.

The extension came after a dominant third campaign in which Wembanyama guided San Antonio to a 62-20 record. The Spurs also captured the Western Conference title and reached their first NBA Finals since 2014, though they ultimately lost to the New York Knicks.

title: Why Seahawks aren't worried about 49ers Deebo Samuel signing
description: The 49ers are banking on that same weapon, now a year older and further from his prime, against the same matchup locksmith for the Seahawks.
fullText:
The San Francisco 49ers brought back wide receiver Deebo Samuel on a one-year deal worth up to $7 million yesterday. Their offseason has been a case of "keeping up with the Joneses" in the NFC West. The Seattle Seahawks are preparing to defend their Super Bowl LX title. The Los Angeles Rams made one of the biggest trades in the history of the sport for Myles Garrett. From Seattle's perspective, though, this should only make them even more excited about where they're at right now.

Skip to the 0:15 mark of this video to see why:

Nick Emmanwori rookie highlights

Future All-Pro pic.twitter.com/hEkWzqYDjr

— NFL Draft Files (@NFL_DF) July 28, 2026

In one of the most iconic plays of his rookie season, Nick Emmanwori dominated Samuel as thoroughly as you'll ever see. The Washington Commanders schemed up a screen for Deebo on 1st-and-10. It came right after Samuel, working out of the slot, caught and ran for a 19-yard gain — the Commanders' biggest play of the night through three quarters. Emmanwori read the play like a book. He blew up his blocker and beat Deebo to the spot for a tackle for loss. The stark difference in athleticism and gameplan in this area of the field was as apparent as it's ever been.

The 49ers are banking on that same weapon, now a year older and further from his prime, against the same matchup locksmith for the Seahawks. He's also a year older, but heading toward his prime instead of leaving it. That math doesn't favor San Francisco.

At this point, Samuel must be a locker-room signing for Shanahan's group. Mike Evans alluded to as much in this press conference yesterday.

Mike Evans on Deebo Samuel signing with the 49ers:

“Deebo is my guy. I met him at the Pro-Bowl in 2021. We hit it off. We were hanging out all week. I love the way he plays the game. I think he’s gonna bring what he brought before to the team. Energy. Versatility. Hell of a… pic.twitter.com/W6uFoffq52

— Coach Yac 🗣 (@Coach_Yac) July 31, 2026

The Seahawks' young, star-studded secondary will face the 49ers' reshaped veteran receiving corps for the first time on October 11. If all parties have a clean bill of health by that point, the age contrast between these two position rooms will be one of the most interesting to see in action this season.

title: Pirates reportedly acquire RP Camilo Doval from Yankees for two prospects
description: New York is getting back 18-year-old Luis Cruz and 22-year-old Omar Alfonzo in the deal.
fullText:
The Pittsburgh Pirates are reportedly acquiring relief pitcher Camilo Doval from the New York Yankees for two prospects, per ESPN's Jeff Passan. The deal is pending a physical for the players involved, per The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal.

New York will reportedly be getting back Luis Cruz and Omar Alfonzo, per the New York Post's Joel Sherman. Alfonzo was Pittsburgh’s No. 17 prospect, per MLB.com. Cruz was not ranked in the top-30 for the organization.

Doval has made 44 appearances for the Yankees this season. He takes a 3-1 record and a 4.54 ERA with him to Pittsburgh.

Doval is known for a plus fastball and has struck out 39 batters in 39.3 innings of work this year. This season, the right-handed reliever has been featuring his sinker most often. Doval has leaned on a sinker, cutter and slider as his three main pitches this year, per Baseball Savant.

The reliever does have a changeup, but has only thrown it 23 times this season (3.4%), and it has largely been out of the zone.

Pittsburgh needed a boost to its bullpen at the trade deadline. The Pirates' pen has registered 24 of the team's 56 losses this season, the fifth-most in MLB. Pittsburgh also has the sixth-most blown saves this year.

New York gets back two unproven prospects. Cruz is 18 years old and can play all three outfield positions. Alfonzo, 22, has split time between being a catcher and a first baseman.

Cruz has only made it to the rookie fall league with Pittsburgh's Black and Gold teams the last two seasons. So far this year, he has played in 17 games and is slashing .313/.460/.396 with seven RBI.

Alfonzo has been on the rise through the Pirates' minor league system this year. He started out in rookie ball, but also played a game in Single-A before spending the majority of the year in Double-A.

The catcher/first baseman has played in 60 games at the Double-A level and is slashing .238/.337/.419 with nine home runs and 35 RBI. He will turn 23 in August.

title: Cincinnati Bengals: Fairfield grad Erick All Jr. found confidence in surviving injury scare on vacation
description: Aug. 1—A scary incident overseas this summer ironically gave Cincinnati Bengals tight end Erick All Jr. the assurance he needed in his comeback from 2024 knee surgery. Now in his first training camp back, the Fairfield High School graduate is anxious to go full throttle while the Bengals are easing him into the mix, despite being fully cleared. All was walking along the sidewalk in Greece when ...
fullText:
Aug. 1—A scary incident overseas this summer ironically gave Cincinnati Bengals tight end Erick All Jr. the assurance he needed in his comeback from 2024 knee surgery.

Now in his first training camp back, the Fairfield High School graduate is anxious to go full throttle while the Bengals are easing him into the mix, despite being fully cleared.

All was walking along the sidewalk in Greece when a three-wheel truck — which he described as similar to a moped — slammed into him, tossing him to the ground. He bounced up with just some scrapes on his face and a couple bumps and bruises.

What could have been a really bad accident actually helped All regain confidence after a brutal first two years in the NFL. Midway through his rookie season in 2024, he retore the ACL he injured in college and missed the entire 2025 campaign as well.

"I got up and was like, 'I'm (expletive) ready, I'm ready,'" All said. "And it didn't hurt me at all. But it just kind of gave me that confidence, like, 'Oh, I'm back.'"

All said the driver had swerved to avoid colliding with someone else as he was about to cross the street, and the three-wheeler ended up hitting him pretty hard, like he was getting blocked by a defensive tackle.

It felt like a football play, but All is used to being the one tossing opponents to the ground.

"That did a lot of good things for the mental, I'm telling you," All said. "Because that's what I do. I'm here for the physicality, and so, you know, after not playing for a while, and I got smacked by that thing, and I got up, 'I'm like, that's as big of a hit that anybody could give.' That's the first time I ever got pancaked, ever, and so I'm like, 'If I can take that, I'm good.' I'm usually the hammer."

All said his friends were stunned he was OK. Maybe it shouldn't have been so surprising.

Bengals coach Zac Taylor has said the physicality that All brings is what makes him such an asset in the tight end room.

"He loves football, and he loves the physical portion of football," Taylor said earlier this summer. "The word 'physical' in the dictionary is a picture of Erick All trying to put his face through somebody's soul, and that's the best way I can describe him."

The Bengals still want to be cautious with All after how much time he's missed from real football, so he's considered "limited," he said. That means he isn't doing special teams yet, but he's been in team and individual drills with the offense.

Just being cleared was a big deal for him.

All participated in the offseason workouts and was doing most activities then, but when he reported July 25 with the rookies and other rehabbing players, he was overjoyed to learn he passed his physical to be cleared in full.

"I had to leave the training room," All said of his reaction to being told he was cleared. "I got teary-eyed for a little bit."

All said he is feeling "great, completely normal," and he had no reservations about getting back into practices. The Bengals aren't in pads until Monday, Aug. 3, but he has surprised his coaches with how willing he has been to get right into the mix.

The hardest part has been not participating in special teams, which he also loves.

"I get we got to be smart," All said. "You can only do so much right away. You got to be smart about things, just in case. But I feel like I'm ready to go, full go. I feel great."

There is still uncertainty over what All will look like in actual games, after so much time away and such a serious knee injury; however, he's been impressive through the first few days of training camp.

All showed a ton of promise in his brief rookie season — playing on a knee that he admits now wasn't fully right — and could be a huge addition to the offense if he's able to perform at that level again.

"It's great to have him back," said Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow. "Obviously, he had a lot going on with his knee, but you wouldn't know it by looking at him. He looks fit, fast, explosive. He'll play a big role for us this year."

title: Root in 'very different place' over Test captaincy
description: England's Joe Root is ready to embrace his second stint as Test captain, saying he is in a "very different place" to when he stepped down from the role four years ago.
fullText:
England's Joe Root is ready to embrace his second stint as Test captain, saying he is in a "very different place" to when he stepped down from the role four years ago.

First appointed captain in 2017, Root led England in a record 64 Tests and oversaw a record 28 wins as skipper before stepping down in April 2022 following a 10-wicket defeat by West Indies.

At that time, England had won just one of their past 17 Tests, including a 4-0 Ashes humbling away in Australia, while also navigating Covid restrictions, with Root admitting the job "took its toll" on his health.

"It had become a very unhealthy relationship, the captaincy and me. I could'nt leave it at the ground any more, it was coming home," Root said in June 2022.

"As soon as I made the decision, I knew it was the right thing to do. I felt like a big weight had been lifted."

Root has sparkled since relinquishing the captaincy, averaging over 54 since June 2022 compared to an average of 46.44 in the five years prior and scoring 16 of his 41 Test centuries.

However, he told BBC Sport he had no doubts when he was offered the opportunity to return to the role by incoming head coach Stephen Fleming, adding the New Zealander's appointment was a big factor in his decision.

Sheffield-born Root, 35, will begin his second stint as full-time captain against Pakistan at Headingley on 19 August, with Fleming joining up with the team ahead of December's tour of South Africa.

"It's one of the greatest honours you could wish to have. I'm very excited by it," Root, who filled the role on an interim basis in June when then captain Ben Stokes missed the second Test against New Zealand following an incident at a nightclub, told BBC Sport.

"I'm in a very different place to the last time I did it with a team in a very different position."

Fleming new England Test coach with Root captain

England captaincy could be what Root needs - Vaughan

On Fleming, who, like Root, holds national records for matches and wins as Test captain, he added: "I've admired him from afar, first as a player and recently as a coach. To get the chance to work together is going to be great fun.

"Once I'd spoken to Stephen about it and saw his energy and excitement for it and saw we're very aligned on it, I got excited very quickly."

Root and Fleming inherit a side in disarray, with series defeats in Australia and at home by New Zealand - which brought criticism of England's carefree playing style - coupled with a run of off-field disciplinary issues bringing the Bazball era to a disappointing conclusion when captain Stokes retired in June and coach Brendon McCullum was sacked a fortnight later.

The duo had previously overseen a resurgence in the Test side, winning 10 of their first 11 matches, and Root hopes he and Fleming can take inspiration from their tenure, rather than starting from scratch.

"Hopefully we can work and build on a lot of the good things that have happened over the last four years," Root said.

"I think Brendon and Ben did a brilliant job, in many ways, of turning things around and getting us in a position where hopefully now we can carry that forward in a slightly different way."

Expanding on his approach to his second captaincy in an in-house interview with the England & Wales Cricket Board, Root said: "The last four years have been the most fun I've had in professional cricket and a big part of that was down to the way they [McCullum and Stokes] got me to see the game.

"Clearly, the last little while is probably what's fresh in everyone's mind but you're looking at a four-year period where we did a lot of amazing things. I've taken a lot from that and I feel it will be a big part of how I want to approach things moving forward as a leader of this team.

"The thing that stands out the most for me is the shift in mindset that was created around how we want to play the game - trying to strip the fear away from things, make sure guys feel that they can really just allow their talent to come out as frequently as possible and in big moments in games. The more that can happen, the better.

"If we can do that alongside recognising when the right time is to put pressure back on teams, or when the right time is to soak it up and to maybe play situations slightly differently, become a little bit smarter in certain areas, then I think we'll be a very formidable team and a very difficult team to break down and to beat."

title: 'Excellent' Liverpool transfer target is now open to exiting his current club
description: Liverpool will be wanting to improve their Premier League standing during the 2026-27 season. The Anfield outfit only mustered up a fifth-place finish last time around which, for a team who were suppo...
fullText:
Liverpool will be wanting to improve their Premier League standing during the 2026-27 season.

The Anfield outfit only mustered up a fifth-place finish last time around which, for a team who were supposed to be defending their title, was a catastrophic result.

The poor performances from most of the Reds' first-team squad led fans to demand that changes were made at Anfield.

And, although the summer window started off pretty well as Liverpool welcomed Jeremy Jacquet and Victor Munoz through the doors, since the Spaniard's arrival, no concrete moves have been made for any other players.

Indeed, rumours about Liverpool preparing a bid for Bradley Barcola have started to emerge but, for now, they're just rumours.

However, one of the Reds' long-linked transfer targets have now had their desire to leave their current club shared which could open the door for Liverpool to swoop in and sign him up.

One of the main areas that Liverpool need to upgrade this summer is their defence.

Virgil van Dijk is now 35 years old and, with Ibrahima Konate now leaving, the Reds' back-line is lacking in depth.

Indeed, Jacquet, Joe Gomez and Giovanni Leoni are all potential options for Liverpool to partner alongside their captain but, with Gomez already out injured and the other two having never played a minute of Premier League football, the Reds' defence is clearly a massive problem.

That's probably one of the many reasons why multiple centre-backs have already been linked with an Anfield switch this summer.

And, even though no move have come to fruition yet, a fresh update from Caught Offside may have just given the green light to Liverpool to try and get a deal over the line for one of their defensive targets.

"Aston Villa centre-back Ezri Konsa is a target for both Arsenal and Liverpool this summer, and he’d be “interested” in a move to the Emirates Stadium," they wrote.

"Liverpool have also been mentioned as potential suitors for Konsa, who seems to be open to leaving Villa Park, even if he’s not currently pushing for the move.

"That leaves Villa in control of the 28-year-old’s situation, so it remains to be seen how things will pan out from here."

Even though Liverpool's centre-backs are certainly an issue, they also have a huge void that they need to fill at right-back.

Not only did they lose Trent Alexander-Arnold at the start of last season but they also signed Jeremie Frimpong to replace him who, after the performances he put in last term, is certainly not a full-back.

And, since Conor Bradley has spent more time on the treatment table than on the pitch recently, he's also unreliable.

This leaves Liverpool with barely any options to choose from at right-back and could force them into using Dominik Szoboszlai or Curtis Jones there instead.

Granted, both of them did fairly well when used as Liverpool's right-back but, if the Reds want to start competing for silverware again, they need natural players in those positions.

That's why Konsa is the perfect signing. The Englishman is a natural centre-back but, as he proved in the 2026 World Cup, he can also be used as a right-back rather effectively.

Indeed, the 'exciting' centre-back is 28 years old so he's a bit older than most of Liverpool's recent targets but, since they've lost so much seniority among their ranks with the departures of Andy Robertson and Mohamed Salah, it feels like some experienced players could be rather useful.

Here's hoping that, even though the Englishman wants to join Arsenal, that Liverpool make their move and get a deal for him over the line.

title: DOJ dropping Reflecting Pool vandalism charge against Olympian David Hearn
description: The DOJ said damage "was the result of flawed installation by the contractor."
fullText:
The Justice Department moved to dismiss the criminal case against Olympian David Hearn, who was alleged to have vandalized the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting pool, acknowledging the damage to the pool "was the result of flawed installation by the contractor."

Hearn pleaded not guilty to a felony destruction of property charge earlier this month after the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro accused him of allegedly "forcefully and violently" ripping up parts of the pool floor.

Pirro's office said in a filing Friday seeking to drop the case that it only learned of evidence pointing to "a rushed and flawed installation process" after Hearn had been indicted by a grand jury.

The filing stated Pirro herself visited the Reflecting Pool on July 17 after it had been fully drained and became aware of significant damage throughout the pool area, which spurred the DOJ to request all documents from the U.S. Interior Department about how the pool was lined.

Olympian David Hearn indicted for alleged vandalism of Reflecting Pool

Those documents indicated a flawed installation by the contractor, Atlantic Industrial Coatings, "with repeated failures of the lining during the installation process, and extensive peeling of the lining throughout the Reflecting Pool" and a rush to complete the renovation project before the America 250 celebration on July 4, according to the filing.

"Because these recently-produced materials significantly undermine the evidentiary basis for the indictment initially supplied by the DOI and U.S. Park Police, the USAO-DC respectively moves to dismiss the indictment without prejudice," the court filing said, meaning the case could be brought again.

The filing includes an email sent on June 11 by a National Park Service engineer to others in the Department of the Interior describing their "concern" that overspray of the new pool coating along the perimeter of the pool could lead to a one-to-two-foot strip "that is vulnerable to peeling."

Some of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool liner appears to be falling apart

That was the area along the perimeter that Hearn was alleged to have pulled up, according to the filing.

At a news conference on July 2 announcing Hearn's indictment, Pirro told reporters that the "the evidence shows and we will prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Hearn willfully destroyed property at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool," and she said the evidence showed that Hearn was observed "forcefully and violently" removing liner material from the bottom of the pool.

The filing from her office on Friday concluded: "Given all of this newly discovered information, it is difficult to attribute the widespread damage to the Reflecting Pool to vandalism, let alone to establish that fact beyond a reasonable doubt."

Attorneys representing Hearn said in a statement Friday that the case against their client should never have been brought.

"Its dismissal today does not erase the abuse of government power in arresting and charging a patriotic American who did nothing wrong. The government's approach was ready, fire, aim," the statement from attorneys Norm Eisen, Mary Dohrmann and Steve Levin said.

"The administration owes Mr. Hearn an apology," they added.

The U.S. attorney's office declined to comment on the dismissal of charges.

It is not known when the judge will make a decision on the U.S. attorney's motion.

Billed as a signature project to beautify Washington, D.C. by President Donald Trump, the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool was plagued with algae and peeling paint since the $16 million renovation of the landmark was completed.

Trump has repeatedly blamed the issues on vandals, including one he said used a boxcutter or knife to make a more than 300-foot gash in the pool.

Reflecting Pool renovations to cost more than $16 million

At the time, five people had been arrested and five others issued federal citations for alleged vandalism at the Reflecting Pool, according to the Interior Department.

On Saturday, the president chastised Pirro in a social media post for dropping the charges, though he acknowledged there may have "been some contractor difficulty" with the project.

"I disagree 100% with Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia, on the Reflecting Pool. I don’t know what she was thinking? To me, it was a pure case of VANDALISM," he wrote.

Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum on Saturday defended his agency and its handling of the investigation, alleging that vandals have "repeatedly caused damage" to the pool.

"We also provided the U.S. Attorney's office expert and eyewitness testimony to the damage done by vandals and provided every piece of evidence they asked for in the requested time line detailing each area of damage at the pool," Burgum said in a social media post.

Atlantic Industrial Coatings was paid more than $14.6 million to resurface the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, according to the most recent federal contracting records.

The company was awarded the contract after a no-bid process in part to expedite the project in time for July 4.

Last month, the company acknowledged in a statement that "some areas in the Reflecting Pool" required repairs.

The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the DOJ's conclusions about the damage to the pool.

ABC News' Peter Charalambous and Emily Change contributed to this report.

title: Newcastle United star Bruno Guimaraes to have Arsenal medical on Monday after £80m deal & five-year contract
description: Arsenal have agreed an £80 million deal to sign Newcastle United midfielder Bruno Guimaraes, according to The Times. The Magpies star is a top target for Gunners manager Mikel Arteta and he is expect...
fullText:
Arsenal have agreed an £80 million deal to sign Newcastle United midfielder Bruno Guimaraes, according to The Times. The Magpies star is a top target for Gunners manager Mikel Arteta and he is expected to have a medical on Monday at London Colney. The Brazilian has signed a five-year contract to join Arsenal, and the Emirates Stadium club could announce his arrival officially next week. Guimaraes is joining the Gunners for an initial £70m, while Newcastle are set to receive a further £10m in add-ons going forward.

His impending arrival will see Christian Norgaard depart after Everton agreed a deal in principle with Arsenal for the midfielder worth about £7m. The North London club were willing to pull all the stops to sign Guimaraes, and they have finally got their man from the look of things.

He will improve their fortunes on the pitch given his attacking prowess from the middle of the park.

The Gunners want to win back-to-back Premier League titles for the first time next term, and adding the Newcastle star to their ranks is a huge boost.

title: Autrey hired as SSU MBB assistant coach
description: Shawnee State men's basketball has announced the addition of Daniel Autrey to its coaching staff. Autrey, a Detroit, Michigan, native, brings a wealth of collegiate playing experience, having competed for five seasons across the junior college, NAIA and NCAA Division II levels. Autrey began his collegiate playing career at Henry Ford College in Dearborn, Michigan, where he competed during the ...
fullText:
Shawnee State men's basketball has announced the addition of Daniel Autrey to its coaching staff.

Autrey, a Detroit, Michigan, native, brings a wealth of collegiate playing experience, having competed for five seasons across the junior college, NAIA and NCAA Division II levels.

Autrey began his collegiate playing career at Henry Ford College in Dearborn, Michigan, where he competed during the 2020-21 and 2021-22 seasons. As a sophomore in 2021-22, he set a program record and ranked second nationally with 109 made three-point field goals.

After two seasons at Henry Ford, Autrey transferred to William Penn for the 2022-23 season. As a junior, he averaged 9.7 points per game over 33 contests while shooting 39.9% from the field and 38.3% from 3-point range.

Autrey then transferred to NCAA Division II member Maryville University, where he redshirted during the 2023-24 campaign. He did not appear in a game during his time with the Saints.

Using his additional year of eligibility, Autrey transferred to West Liberty for the 2024-25 season as a graduate student. In 35 games with the Hilltoppers, he averaged 7.0 points per game while shooting 80-of-190 (.421) from the field, 67-of-172 (.390) from 3-point range and 17-of-19 (.895) from the free-throw line.

"Daniel brings exceptional basketball IQ and will elevate our game on both ends of the floor," said Fred Lymas, Shawnee State's men's basketball head coach. "Which is fitting for someone who was named one of the top two-guards in the country during his playing career."

Shawnee State's season opener is scheduled for Wednesday, Nov. 11, when the Bears host Simmons College at 1 p.m. inside Waller Gymnasium.

title: I Stop LLMs Drifting in Production Codebases
description:
The problem I care about with LLM coding is drift: one plausible
shortcut gets copied, then future sessions start treating it as how
the app...
fullText:
The problem I care about with LLM coding is drift: one plausible
shortcut gets copied, then future sessions start treating it as how
the app works. I’ve used AI coding tools every day as a team lead on
large private client codebases, across features, bug fixes, refactors,
reviews, and more recently a finance workflow processing more than
$20m a month in capital. When the app has audit trails, permissions,
calculations, generated documents, client workflows, and operational
handoffs, “prompt harder” is not an engineering system. What works for
me is guardrails in the repo: checks, docs, lint rules, tool-call
blockers, and handoff validation that stop the model drifting before
the mistake becomes normal.

That starts with establishing good patterns first. LLMs are pattern
followers before they are engineers. They look for the nearest example
that appears to work, then continue from there. If the repo is full of
clean service boundaries, narrow components, cited docs, targeted
invalidation, and boring validation commands, the model has something
useful to copy. If the repo is full of shortcuts, the model will copy
those too, just faster.

This post is the practical version of that system. I’ll cover the
layers I use, why they exist, where they should be strict, where they
should start as warnings, and a few examples toward the end that you
can steal without building my exact setup.

For a long time the only thing stopping the model from making a mess
was me typing “please follow the architecture” again. That is not a
workflow. That is me supervising a process, and I have already done
enough of that.

LLMs are very good at local optimisation. They look at the current
file, the nearest import, the most obvious pattern, and the shape of
the request. Then they move fast. That is useful when the local
pattern is good, and dog shite when the local pattern is temporary,
legacy, copied from a spike, or just wrong.

So I moved the guardrails to places the model cannot politely forget:

That is the difference between advice and pressure. Advice says “try
not to use $effect”. Pressure says “this .svelte file was not
modified because the write contained $effect; rewrite it with $derived, an event handler, an action, or a lifecycle API”. One of
those scales, the other becomes review debt.

I queried my Pi session history for one private production codebase
where I’ve been deliberately building this system.

Those numbers are not a benchmark. They’re just receipts that the
rails were in the normal path.

The useful bit is that the failures were real. The checks caught
things like:

That is what I want from AI-assisted development. Not a model that
never makes mistakes, because that does not exist, but a system where
common mistakes are cheap, loud, and boring to fix.

The most obvious example for me is Svelte’s $effect. LLMs love it.
It looks familiar to them, it smells like React’s effect hook, and it
is an easy escape hatch when the model has not worked out whether the
value should be derived, handled in an event, pushed into an action,
or dealt with through lifecycle code.

The problem is that once $effect lands, it becomes a pattern. The
next session sees it. Then another one copies it. Then the codebase
has five examples of using it, which sets the pattern going forward.

I watched this happen in a production session. The agent found two
components using $state and $effect, treated them as the
established pattern, then used the same approach in three more
components. A few minutes later, another $effect appeared to move a
value into form state.

The individual changes looked reasonable in isolation. The problem was
the direction of travel. Each new example made the pattern look more
intentional to the next session, which meant I was having the same
conversation again instead of improving the codebase.

So I added a guardrail to my-pi for this:

The package watches agent tool calls. If an agent tries to write,
edit, or bash-write a .svelte file containing $effect, the tool
call can be blocked before the file is created or modified.

The important part is the timing. This is not a review comment after
the bad code exists. It’s not a hook to “remember, please prefer $derived”. It is the harness not allowing the code to be written.

That gives me three adoption modes:

The blocked message also matters. It should tell the model exactly
what happened:

The wording came from testing the first version. The guardrail blocked
the write correctly, but the agent still reported that it had created
the file. In another test, it started investigating the block rather
than carrying on with one of the suggested alternatives.

That showed me the message needed to do more than explain the rule. It
also needed to describe the result of the tool call and give the agent
a clear next step. The code stopped the write; the extra context
helped the agent recover and continue the task.

Agents are very good at saying “done” after a failed tool call. The
guardrail has to make the failed write explicit so the model continues
the task instead of summarising imaginary progress.

And this is not Svelte-specific as an idea. Anyone can build the same
kind of Pi plugin for their own stack:

Swap $effect for whatever the team keeps fighting over:

I don’t think $effect is evil. I think repeated prompts are a bad
way for me to enforce a rule I already know I want.

Tool-call blocking is great for patterns I want to stop immediately.
For everything else, I like custom lint rules.

Generic linting catches generic mistakes. It does not know the
project’s taste: that project-owned identifiers should be snake_case, that file names should be kebab-case, that broad cache
invalidation should not be used casually, or that a Svelte effect
needs an explanation if it is genuinely allowed. So I encode that.

Mine is an oxlint JS plugin with four rules:

The smallest one catches the broad-invalidation problem from that
list:

The $effect rule can be more nuanced at the lint layer than the tool
layer. The tool boundary blocks the write outright. Lint lets the
effect through if there is a real explanation next to it:

previous_comment_text is just sourceCode.getCommentsBefore(node) filtered to comments within three lines of the call. Two thresholds
are the whole rule: the comment has to match something effect-shaped,
and it has to be at least 24 characters. Without that length check // effect would count as a justification.

That comment requirement does two things. It makes the human author
justify the escape hatch, and it gives future LLM sessions a better
example to copy: the model sees that effects are not thrown around,
they come with a reason.

Same thing for broad invalidation. The model does not need a
philosophical discussion about cache invalidation. It needs the repo
to reject the lazy option and point at the expected one.

Lint rules are good for per-file patterns. Architecture drift usually
needs more context.

For that, I like a tools/check-boundaries.ts script that runs as
part of pnpm check.

The script scans tracked source files and fails on project-specific
boundary violations. Things like:

Most of that is just string checks, file paths, and a bit of
TypeScript AST traversal. There is no clever rule engine underneath.
It walks every import in every tracked file and runs a flat list of if statements:

is_web_route and is_service_module are path predicates in a path-rules.ts file, and they are exactly as dumb as they sound.
Workspace-to-workspace rules need one extra step, resolving the
relative specifier before comparing:

Then I wire it into the normal path:

With that in place, the model cannot claim the work is complete
without the check disagreeing.

My boundary checks were all born from pain. I did not sit down and
design a perfect architecture rule engine. I started with the thing
the model kept doing wrong, and the useful ones have been these.

Routes are tempting. The model is already in a +page.server.ts file,
it sees a data need, and it reaches for the database. That is exactly
how route files become orchestration soup.

The guardrail says routes call services or commands. Database access
lives behind the server boundary where it can be tested, authorised,
and reused.

A model will quite happily mutate the local object if it makes the UI
update. That might make a demo feel alive, but on a real app it skips
the server command, audit event, permissions, validation, and
persistence path.

So the boundary check looks for assignments and mutating array methods
on known domain roots in route files. If it finds them, it fails with
a boring message:

LLMs love placeholder data. Fake email domains, avatar services,
synthetic attachments, seeded arrays in route components. Fine for a
mockup. Dangerous when the file is production-shaped.

This check is the least sophisticated thing in the repo and it has
earned its place. It is a list of regexes and a loop:

The new_id( one matters more than it looks. A route generating its
own business identifier means the model skipped the server command
that was supposed to issue it.

The escape hatch is the @allow-demo-data comment, and it has to
carry a replacement note. That turns demo leakage from “oops, missed
it in review” into “the check failed before handoff”.

With SvelteKit remote functions, the model will often put schemas,
handlers, and remote bindings wherever it happens to be editing. A
boundary check can enforce the shape:

That keeps the server-safe shape predictable. More importantly, it
keeps future examples clean for the next agent session.

Not everything should be a hard failure on day one. For large route
components and state modules, I prefer advisories first.

The trick I landed on is not tripping on any single metric. I count a
few, then only advise when more than one is out of range:

A 300 line component that is otherwise simple stays quiet. A 300 line
component with eight buttons and three forms does not. The metrics
themselves are boring: line_count, a TypeScript AST walk counting
functions and $state calls, and source.match(/<form\b/g) for the
markup.

The advisory names the doc it wants you to read, which is the bit that
makes it useful to an agent rather than just to me.

The check can pass while still making the smell visible. Later, when
the team is ready, a strict mode promotes advisories to hard failures:

That gives me a ratchet: warn first, fix opportunistically, enforce
once the pattern is understood.

Docs are not enough. LLMs skim. They read the first heading, decide
they understand the architecture, then confidently invent the rest.

So what I want is not “we have docs”, it is “the agent has a
repeatable way to retrieve the right docs before making a risky
change”.

I do not care whether that is SQLite FTS, ripgrep, a wiki, embeddings,
or something else. The mechanics can be simple:

The important part is the rule around it:

If the work touches business rules, permissions, data flow, release
behaviour, or calculations, cite the source-of-truth doc before
implementing.

Not “I checked the docs”, but the actual file, the actual section, the
actual decision. That is the difference between a claim and evidence.

This catches a lot of hallucinated implementation, because the model
has to ground the change in something outside its own confident
waffle. It also gives reviewers a much better handoff:

That is reviewable in a way that “updated the approval flow” never is.

A skill is not a magic prompt. It is a small playbook for a repeated
workflow, and the value is entirely in how narrow it is. “Write clean
code, follow best practices, test your work” is wallpaper. This is
not:

That matters because LLM sessions do not share judgement. One session
might learn the right pattern after three failed attempts, but unless
I write it down, the next session starts from vibes again. Project
skills turn those little lessons into reusable operating procedure,
and I lean on them most for:

Agents love a confident handoff. Sometimes it is deserved. Sometimes
the last command failed, there are untracked files everywhere, and the
model is still saying “all set”. So the handoff needs rails too, and a
simple docs/agent-handoff.md does a lot of that work:

Not glamorous, but it removes the ambiguity. For release-shaped work,
I bundle the checks:

If the app has generated artefacts, exported client builds, generated
infrastructure, or sanitised release repos, those get verification
scripts too. The ones I keep reaching for:

That is the layer I skipped for longest. Lint, some tests, then still
letting the agent summarise the work with no evidence behind it. The
final handoff is part of the system, and I treat it like one now. It’s
the same instinct behind how I work with LLMs: validate the
claim, not the effort.

None of this needed a whole internal platform up front. I added one
guardrail per failure mode, roughly in this order.

If agents keep writing a pattern you hate, block or warn on it at the
tool boundary. For Svelte, mine was $effect in .svelte writes. For
another stack it might be:

Start in warn mode if you are nervous. Move to block when the
false positives are understood.

Pick the rule you are tired of repeating in review. Mine was this one:

Implement that one and wire it into pnpm check. I did not wait for
the perfect AST version. A slightly blunt check that catches a real
mistake beats a beautiful architecture diagram the model ignores.

Some patterns are allowed, but only with context, and that is where
explanation rules help:

This makes the exception visible and gives future agents a better
example.

Then enforce it in review and handoff. If there is no source-of-truth
doc, that is the finding.

If a rule is useful but too noisy, make it an advisory first. Large
route components, too many actions in a route server file, a huge
state module: all advisories to start with. Then add a strict mode
when the team is ready.

That keeps the system humane. Guardrails should reduce review debt,
not create a different flavour of misery.

Guardrails can be annoying. They catch things that are technically
fine. They need allowlists. They occasionally block a clever solution
because the rule is deliberately boring.

That is the trade, and I’ll take a few boring false positives over a
codebase where every AI session gets to invent the architecture again.

The trick is keeping the rules close to observed failure modes. I do
not encode my entire engineering philosophy. I encode the stuff the
model actually keeps getting wrong.

When a review comment repeats three times, I make it a rule. When a
rule turns out to be noisy, I drop it to an advisory. When an advisory
keeps catching real problems, I promote it. When a rule stops earning
its keep, I delete it.

That is not bureaucracy. It is maintenance of the path.

LLMs make teams faster, but speed compounds the system around it.

If the repo has no memory, no source of truth, no examples, no
validation, and no automated way to say “no, that crosses a boundary”,
the model will still move fast. It will just move fast in every
direction.

I am not trying to stop the LLM writing code. I am trying to stop it
turning every local shortcut into tomorrow’s architecture.

So the guardrails go where the model has to hit them:

That is how I keep the useful part of AI-assisted development without
drowning the team in cleanup.

Make the right path easier to follow than the wrong one.
