fullText:
Just past 10 a.m. on Wednesday, a delegation of Saudi officials arrived at the West Wing carrying a message for the White House.

Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, on an unannounced visit to Washington, conveyed word to both President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance from his brother, the kingdom's powerful crown prince, that Saudi Arabia wants the Iran war to deescalate — and that prolonging the conflict carries major risks, according to people familiar with the conversations.

A day earlier, another emissary had arrived through the same door with a different message. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, sitting with Trump in the Oval Office, voiced skepticism that diplomacy with Iran would prove fruitful, according to Israeli officials. Instead, the two discussed options for pressuring Iran, including renewing a full-scale war, those officials said.

The back-to-back meetings this week were scheduled coincidentally. But they nonetheless underscore the crosscurrents facing Trump as he seeks an exit ramp to a conflict that has extended well past his deadline.

As pressure mounts from fellow Republicans to wind the war down, it actually appears to be expanding, with new fronts opening up and virtually every country in the region now drawn in. Efforts at diplomacy are halting at best; a senior US official said resuming direct diplomacy with Iran does not appear imminent.

Despite Trump's claims Iran is "begging" for a deal to end the violence, some US officials fear regime figures appear more committed than ever to wielding leverage over the Strait of Hormuz and firing missiles toward American troops.

Trump has grown frustrated at Tehran's unwillingness to bend to his demands, leading to angry meetings behind the scenes and expletive-laced phone calls to his allies, according to US officials. He convened his Cabinet on Friday at Camp David, perhaps hoping to seize inspiration from the retreat's past role in successful Middle East diplomacy.

"I think we just want to win," the president said when asked how he planned to revive the stalled diplomatic efforts, offering few clues of how he intends to proceed. "They'll get weaker. They'll get a little stronger maybe now. Then they'll get weaker. And then they'll peter out."

The ongoing threats from Iran have forced Trump to alter his own plans, most notably a swap in Air Force One aircraft on his return trip from Turkey earlier this month. The change was made amid ramped up threats from neighboring Iran, according to officials, and subsequent coverage of the issue infuriated and embarrassed the president.

Many of Trump's allies are now worried the Iran war is threatening to engulf his presidency entirely, and with it, Republicans' chances in upcoming midterm elections, according to some GOP operatives. A CNN survey this week found only 28% of Americans approved of his handling of the war.

Options for escalating the conflict have been presented to Trump and debated at length, and more military assets flowed to the region in anticipation of a go-ahead from the president. One plan conceived by Central Command would involve heavy bombardment over the course of one or two weeks to take out Iran's missile capabilities, US officials said.

Asked Friday whether he planned to "go big" in escalation, Trump said he'd already gone that route. "We're going big. We've already gone big," he insisted.

During a hearing on Capitol Hill last week, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine acknowledged that it is unlikely Trump can accomplish all his previously stated objectives for the war with air bombing alone.

"Air power has its limits," Caine told lawmakers at the time.

And Trump has so far held off, in part after hearing concerns from Caine about dwindling supplies of air defense interceptors. Other officials have also raised worries about the risks of high civilian casualties if Trump followed through on threats to strike infrastructure sites like bridges and water desalination plants.

"Who am I hurting there? I'm hurting the people, so I'm not looking to do that," the president said during a Fox News interview this week.

At this point, diplomatic discussions among regional players revolve around a short-term agreement focused on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, according to people familiar with the discussions, that would allow Trump to claim a win. The waterway has become the center of the conflict after the US and Iran came away with very different interpretations of how the issue was addressed in last month's memorandum of understanding.

Republicans, who have largely supported Trump over the course of the conflict but are increasingly concerned higher gas prices could hurt their party in the midterms, have conveyed in private conversations the importance of getting the conduit reopened, the GOP operatives said.

"Obviously, we want success there. We think that we've achieved a high level of military success there," Senate Majority Leader John Thune said this week. "The question on the Strait of Hormuz is something that obviously the president and his team are trying to continue to negotiate, and hopefully they'll land an outcome or a solution there in the near future."

The White House said Iran would "continue to pay" until they come to the table in a way Trump accepts. "The United States signed an MOU with Iran and they broke it, shot at commercial ships, and killed American soldiers. President Trump is not going to stand by and allow this terrorist behavior to occur. Iran will continue to pay until they come to the table in, what President Trump deems, a meaningful way," press secretary Karoline Leavitt said in a statement.

While mediators including Qatar and Pakistan are hurriedly working to revive diplomatic talks, there are few signs of any active negotiations. Instead, officials now fear Iran's powerful revolutionary guards are firmly in control of the decision making, leaving the political figures the US has been talking with as figureheads.

Complicating matters are the internal dynamics of the IRGC itself, where a handful of senior commanders are all jockeying for control. That dynamic is a leading reason why US officials and regional partners fear the conflict is likely to drag on.

In the Oval Office this week, Trump hinted at the divide, saying attempted Iranian strikes at US positions had not been the work of the interlocutors his team is trying to engage.

"It was a different group than we're dealing with," he insisted. "They've already apologized."

Trump has complained that it's difficult to know who is making decisions inside Iran, and he sometimes casts doubt on the ability of the US and Tehran to arrive at any agreement.

"People want to talk, but they break their words so often," he said Friday at Camp David. "All they do is make me angry. You know, they just make me angry."

Still, his top envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner have voiced confidence a deal is possible.

During Trump's meeting with Netanyahu this week — attended by Witkoff and other senior officials — the prime minister appeared skeptical that diplomacy with Iran would work, and told Trump as much, according to Israeli officials familiar with the meeting.

Instead, the men discussed various options for ramping up pressure on Iran, including intensifying military strikes and economic measures. Netanyahu assured Trump in the meeting that the US president was the final decision maker, one of the officials said, seeking to rebut suggestions Israel is attempting to sway Trump toward a resumption of war.

"We're talking about what to do – you don't have a textbook solution," an Israeli official who attended the meeting said afterward.

The next day, Trump's visitor from Saudi Arabia offered the kingdom's own assessment of the conflict. The visit by Prince Khalid — a close confidant of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Saudi Arabia's de facto ruler — was brief and initially scheduled for last week. He departed Washington soon after leaving the White House.

Despite new joint US-Saudi operations against Iran-backed militias in Iraq this week, Saudi Arabia still wants to see de-escalation in the conflict, the defense minister told Vance, according to people familiar with the conversation. The Saudi military action was meant to make clear that it will defend itself and that attacking its civilian infrastructure is a red line that will not go unanswered, the sources said. It was also meant to send the message to Iran's proxies that this is not their war to fight.

Saudi Arabia's assessment, according to the sources, is that Iran will seek to create leverage through escalation, and continue trying to use pro-Iranian militias in Iraq and Yemen to do so.

"The minister's underlying message … is that it's Netanyahu who is pushing for this escalation, whereas the Kingdom wants to de-escalate," a source familiar with the conversation told CNN.

What Trump took away from the meetings wasn't exactly clear, though he claimed hours later the widening conflict — now involving new players like Egypt and Saudi Arabia — would soon come to a resolution.

"It's going to be straightening out," he said Wednesday, going on to preview another night of retaliatory strikes: "It's our turn, and we'll see if we get there with an agreement at some point. But we're going to hit them very hard."

This story has been updated with additional developments.

title: 'We can have seven homes or we can have 70.' In wake of Los Angeles wildfires, homeowners and developers clash
description: Many LA wildfire survivors are united against 'predatory developers,' who they say are exploiting vulnerable residents and changing their communities. Lawmakers are trying to balance the need to build...
fullText:
LOS ANGELES — After the Eaton fire tore through Neil Tyler's home in Altadena, he and his wife quickly set out to rebuild.

They designed their new house to resemble the old one and, with the framing complete, expect to return in the spring.

But recently the 41-year-old attorney discovered a developer's plans to build 10 houses on a neighboring lot. It is one of more than a dozen such proposals Tyler said he and other residents have identified. If allowed to go forward, he worries the projects will encourage more developers to follow with a sea of subdivisions, erasing the patchwork of quirky, tight-knit neighborhoods that defined Altadena before the blaze.

"I can't foresee ever feeling like we've recaptured the dream house," Tyler said. "Because it's not just the house, it's the community we fell in love with."

The distrust of what Tyler calls "predatory developers" has united wildfire survivors from Altadena's foothills to the winding streets of Pacific Palisades and the Malibu coastline, which were equally devastated in last year's blazes.

And it has spilled into the recovery's politics.

State lawmakers are pursuing a new round of limits on denser rebuilding, arguing that developers are taking advantage of special rules never meant for them. The effort comes after Gov. Gavin Newsom, pushed by residents to curb investor activity, issued an executive order last summer banning a state duplex law in Pacific Palisades.

"The disaster survivor who literally was living in a home that is now gone through no fault of their own deserves a little bit more grace than an opportunistic investor," said Ben Allen, a Democratic state senator representing Pacific Palisades and parts of Malibu. "There's a special status for these folks who lost everything."

Yet these proposals are colliding with California's broader drive for more housing amid a long-running shortage and the realities of a frustrating rebuild that is unfolding slowly as homeowners struggle to cover daunting construction costs. Developers working in the burn zones say they're building housing that survivors will want and that broader Los Angeles needs. And some victims of the wildfires worry that attempts to reel in developers could depress property values or complicate opportunities to build additional homes on their properties.

Developers often become flashpoints in the aftermath of natural disasters, said Zachary Lamb, an assistant professor of city and regional planning at University of California, Berkeley. Tensions emerge with the need to attract investment and know-how to restore homes and businesses, he said.

"Developers obviously have a profit motive that's built into their work. But they also have expertise," said Lamb, who has studied post-Katrina New Orleans and other recoveries.

The January 2025 Eaton and Palisades fires destroyed 16,000 homes, businesses and other structures, burning a stretch of beachfront houses along the iconic Pacific Coast Highway in Malibu and one of Los Angeles' centers of Black homeownership in Altadena. The significance of these and other areas intensified concerns that land grabs could produce pricey, out-of-scale houses or leave lots vacant as investors wait for values to rise.

Within weeks of the fires, "Not For Sale" signs popped up on charred lots, giving rise to a rallying cry in Altadena and Pacific Palisades. Anxiety has escalated as homeowners, particularly in Altadena, have been bombarded with unsolicited offers from real estate investors looking to buy their properties. When LA Mayor Karen Bass celebrated the first completed rebuild in Pacific Palisades in December, survivors howled in protest because it was a spec house.

And as lot sales have increased, so too has concern over the role developers and outside investors will have in the rebuild. More than 1,000 vacant lots — about 10 percent of those that burned — have been sold in Pacific Palisades and Altadena as of June, according to an analysis from real estate firm Redfin. Half the sales have gone to investors, the data shows, with their share rising over time.

Tyler and hundreds of his neighbors packed an emergency Altadena Town Council meeting in June to share their indignation over, among other things, the fact that state laws meant to spur denser building had been shelved in wealthier Pacific Palisades but not Altadena.

State Sen. Sasha Renée Pérez, a Democrat who represents Altadena, responded with SB 1090, which would pause the construction of duplexes, and 10-unit subdivisions, such as the one planned near Tyler's home, in the community during the recovery. Lawmakers are expected to debate the bill when they return to the Capitol following summer recess next week.

"It will protect Eaton fire survivors and allow them the time they need to rebuild their community without the overpowering influence of predatory developers," Pérez said at a Sacramento rally this month.

But developers say the anger at them is misplaced.

Sean Beddoe, co-owner of Stone West Homes, said the subdivision law makes it possible for companies like his to produce starter homes for survivors and other Los Angeles buyers. Stone West has bought seven lots in Altadena and wants to put up about 10 houses averaging 1,750 square feet on each.

Beddoe said the company was encouraged to pursue its plans in part by a brochure put out by Los Angeles County that touted the rebuilding opportunities in Altadena under the subdivision law, SB 1123. Then in the spring, he said, county planners abruptly stopped the permitting process. The developer has since sued over the decision. (County officials say they voided three permit applications for subdivisions and are not accepting new ones after consulting the state housing department and concluding the law doesn't apply to lots surrounded by other vacant parcels.)

The uncertainty has led Stone West to abandon plans to buy two more lots, including the one behind Tyler's home.

If its SB 1123 projects cannot proceed, Beddoe said, the company will build large, expensive single-family homes instead.

"We can have seven homes or we can have 70 homes," Beddoe said. "So the question is, which one helps the neighborhood recover from the fire more?"

Beddoe said profit does not make developers' role illegitimate.

"The guy that cleared the lots, the guy that cut down the trees that were burnt, the guy that swept the streets after the fires, all these people made money," he said. "That doesn't mean what they were doing was wrong. We are simply trying to build homes in a city that has a massive housing shortage."

Concerns about investor influence are playing out along the coast as well.

New Zealand billionaire toy magnates Nick and Mat Mowbray have spent $111 million on 16 burned lots along Pacific Coast Highway, according to LA county records. The brothers want to manufacture prefabricated luxury homes at their factory in China and ship them to Malibu where they'll be assembled on site, said Marcel Fontijn, their U.S. representative.

Fontijn said the brothers love Malibu and plan to keep one house for themselves, while selling the others.

"Every single home across the 16 lots will be individually custom-designed to match its specific site conditions and preserve the unique architectural identity of the Malibu coastline," Fontjin said.

Still, he's acknowledged the skepticism of their plans.

"When you hear 'foreign investor', when you hear 'China-built housing' — these are two things that you don't want to hear in your neighborhood," Fontijn told Realtor.com last fall.

Malibu residents have reacted to the Mowbrays' plans with indignation and incredulity. The brothers are using state laws that allow property owners in disaster zones to increase the size of rebuilt homes by 10 percent without undergoing additional review from local and state regulators.

Citing the Mowbrays, Allen has introduced legislation, SB 1229, to give those regulators greater oversight for such rebuilds along the coast — but only if the builder isn't the original owner.

"The main reason we want to speed up the rebuild process is because of deep sympathy for the folks who lost their homes," he said. "Now you're seeing developers coming through, trying to buy up some of this property and take advantage of the waived permitting requirements."

Survivors fear land purchases by developers with ready capital will continue to accelerate as neighbors abandon plans to return. Financing gaps, dwindling insurance payouts, costly labor and materials and delays in securing long-term federal recovery funding have all complicated rebuilding for residents.

At the same time, the situation has evolved into more complicated views about density and the role of developers.

Some Altadena residents initially wary of investors changed their minds after watching one firm complete well-appointed homes.

And survivors in both communities are taking advantage of permissive state laws to add units to their own properties. More than one-third of permit applications in Altadena include at least one accessory dwelling unit as do one in five applications in Pacific Palisades, according to a POLITICO analysis of rebuilding data.

Shirley Weaver Taylor, who bought her home in Altadena in 1979, has relied on the state's duplex law, SB 9, to build a second home where her 500-square-foot garage once stood. With it nearly completed, she plans to rent the unit to relatives or close friends while living in the rebuilt main house.

Taylor, 77, understands the concerns about developers in Altadena, but called Pérez's legislation to ban SB 9 "a big mistake."

The law, she said, gives, "the common man and woman the opportunity to do something."

The proposals to limit denser projects in LA fire zones face an uncertain future.

In December, the pro-development group YIMBY Law sued over Newsom's executive order that banned SB 9 duplexes in Pacific Palisades and other highest-risk fire areas. Malibu and Pasadena used the order to prohibit duplexes in its neighborhoods affected by the Palisades and Eaton fires, respectively.

But now officials in both cities are taking steps to reverse that decision as part of a proposed settlement. The lawsuit remains pending for Pacific Palisades.

YIMBY organizations, which have gained influence as part of the push for growth in Sacramento, also are opposing Pérez's bill, arguing that the density laws can help underinsured owners rebuild and ease the housing shortage. Newsom, meanwhile, has signaled he may not be keen to sign Allen's bill if it makes it to his desk. The governor has repeatedly criticized the California Coastal Commission for impeding development, and Allen's legislation would give the commission additional regulatory authority.

POLITICO Data/Graphics Editor Sean McMinn contributed to this report.

title: ICE lodges detainer on Salvadoran national, 18, accused of 2 fatal shootings in Houston
description: ICE lodged an ice detainer against Jefferson Adonay Velasquez-Torres, who came here illegally from El Salvador in 2014 and is charged with two murders in Houston.
fullText:
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security on Friday said Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) had lodged a detainer asking Texas to not release an El Salvadoran national, who is accused of murder in two fatal shootings and is in the country illegally, without notifying the agency.

Jefferson Adonay Velasquez-Torres, 18, was charged this week with murder for an April 27 shooting outside a Houston nightclub in which Noah Ramirez, 27, died.

Two others were injured in the shooting, according to a report from affiliate FOX 26 Houston.

Ice Arrests More Than 900 Suspected Human Traffickers During Fifa World Cup, Rescues 180 Victims: Dhs

Velasquez-Torres was previously charged in June with murder for his alleged involvement in a shooting at a Houston house party last August that left Angel Garcia, 17, dead.

A second suspect, Enrique Aguilar, 19, was also arrested in connection with Garcia's death, FOX 26 reported.

Twice-deported Illegal Immigrant Accused Of Firing Toward Texas Homes During Neighborhood Dispute

Velasquez-Torres also faces charges of unlawfully carrying a weapon and aggravated robbery.

The 18-year-old came into the U.S. illegally as a minor in 2014 during former President Barack Obama's second term and was released into the country.

"This criminal illegal alien has been charged with TWO counts of murder after two fatal shootings in Houston," Homeland Security Assistant Secretary Lauren Bis said in a statement.

Video Shows Ice Officers Arresting Alleged Ms-13 Gang Member, A 'Known Suspected Terrorist' In Florida

She continued, "He would not be in our country if it weren't for the reckless open-border policies of the Obama Administration. ICE asked officials in Texas to not release this heinous murderer from jail without notifying ICE. Thankfully, Texas cooperates with us and together we will ensure this public safety threat will never be loose on our streets."

Velasquez-Torres is being held in the Harry County Jail after being denied bond for charges related to the second shooting.

title: World-renowned mountaineer Nirmal Purja confirmed dead after Pakistan avalanche
description: The famed Nepalese climber Nirmal Purja – who made history over the years by trekking some of the world’s highest peaks – has been confirmed dead after an avalanche struck an expedition in the Himalay...
fullText:
The famed Nepalese climber Nirmal Purja – who made history over the years by trekking some of the world's highest peaks – has been confirmed dead after an avalanche struck an expedition in the Himalayas earlier this week.

Purja "tragically lost his life" following the landslide, according to a social media post on Saturday published by the Nimsdai Foundation, which he founded in 2022. "Today, we mourn not only Nims, but every life lost in this tragedy including his trusted climbing partners and guides," the Instagram post read.

"His legacy will live on in the countless lives he changed and the people he inspired to climb their own mountains," the post added.

Forty-three-year-old Purja was among 10 mountaineers who went missing on Thursday after they were believed to have been on 8,047-meter-tall Broad Peak, in northern Pakistan, when a landslide hit around midday local time.

At least four people have been confirmed dead, including Purja, the Omani climber Nadhira Al Harthy, the Nepali climber Pur Bahadur Gurung "Yukta" and the US climber Sarah Mallory Geis.

Purja's foundation said "other members of the expedition sadly did not survive" without giving details and there has been no confirmation from authorities.

Recovery efforts for the six remaining climbers are ongoing. Earlier on Saturday, emergency workers had raised concerns to CNN over the prospect of another avalanche falling and hampering the operation

One Pakistani mountaineer warned the remaining climbers' chances of survival "are very slim now." "Pakistani mountains are very different to Nepal," Naila Kiani, a spokesperson for the Pakistan Alpine Club, told the BBC on Saturday.

"Some of those areas are still avalanche prone, so our rescue team has to be very careful to assess whether they are endangering their lives," she added.

Purja, a former British army soldier, raised the profile of climbing on the world stage by repeatedly breaking records as a measure of endurance. In 2019, he made history by climbing all of the world's 14 peaks over 8,000 meters (26,300 feet) – dubbed by NASA as the Eight Thousanders – in just over six months.

Kiani, who previously climbed with Purja, described him as "very fearless" and said that "he made the impossible happen."

In an interview in 2019, Purja told CNN that he wanted to use his platform to honor the skills of Nepal's Sherpa people. "Even though they were top climbers, they didn't get the right recognition," Purja said. "Hopefully, I thought I could uplift their names."

Al Harthy, the Omani mountaineer who died on Thursday, also previously spoke to CNN, describing her ambition to climb one of the Eight Thousanders. She used her profile to empower other Muslim women and girls – including her 32 nieces – to take on endurance sports.

"Our faith … it makes you stand up again. It gives you strength, it gives you power," Al Harthy said in 2021. "(My nieces) are very strong, and they stand up for their rights," she added. "I always wake up in the morning and say, 'Alhumdullilah, thank God I'm here.'"

CNN's Lex Harvey, Ross Adkin and Xiaoqian Lin contributed reporting.

title: Gold sculptures, Rose Garden statues, and paintings of Trump: All of the new artwork Trump has added to the White House
description: Donald Trump has added new paintings and sculptures to the White House — some from the White House Collection, and others from contemporary artists.
fullText:
President Donald Trump has added numerous new paintings and sculptures to the White House.

Some pieces are from the White House Collection, and others were acquired from contemporary artists.

Trump's assassination attempt has inspired multiple pieces of White House artwork.

Among the sweeping changes President Donald Trump has made to the White House during his second, non-consecutive term, one is a particular interest in curating its artwork.

He has added five new statues to the White House Rose Garden, covered the Oval Office in gold pieces and presidential portraits from the White House Collection, and hung photos and paintings of himself in several rooms.

When reached for comment, White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Business Insider, "President Trump continues to implement long-overdue and necessary renovations to beautify the People's House as we celebrate our great Nation's 250th anniversary of independence."

"Thanks to the Builder-in-Chief, the White House will be properly glorified and remain in excellent condition for generations to come," Ingle said.

Here's a look at the artwork that Trump has added to the White House.

In the Cross Hall, Trump replaced a portrait of President Barack Obama with one of himself painted by artist Marc Lipp in April 2025.

The painting depicts his defiant response following an assassination attempt at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania.

Also that month, a portrait of Trump was placed between two first ladies' portraits.

The portrait of Trump was painted by Elena Ruseva, who works under the name MAGA Langelo.

Trump also uses the painting, in which his face is overlaid with an American flag, as his Truth Social profile photo. It's titled "Free America. Trump."

In May 2025, a statue depicting Trump's attempted assassination in Butler, Pennsylvania, was displayed next to the Resolute Desk.

A group called the Trump Statue Project is raising funds for a 9-foot version of the statue by sculptor Stan Watts.

In July 2025, Trump redecorated the Cabinet Room with artwork from the White House Collection and gold medallions.

The Cabinet Room was sparsely decorated in previous administrations. In July 2025, Trump told reporters he had selected presidential portraits from the White House Vault to display in the Cabinet Room and was "very proud of it."

Trump said he chose a portrait of James K. Polk because he was "a very good president" and "a real estate guy," and added portraits of George Washington, John Adams, Andrew Jackson, Abraham Lincoln, Franklin D. Roosevelt, and Dwight Eisenhower.

Trump added photos of himself with world leaders, including Russian President Vladimir Putin, to the Palm Room in September 2025.

The Palm Room serves as a lobby connecting the Rose Garden to the Oval Office.

The black-and-white photo hanging in the bottom right was taken by White House photographer Daniel Torok and is on display at the National Portrait Gallery in Washington, DC.

In October 2025, Trump acquired a bronze sculpture of an eagle atop Article I of the US Constitution for the Oval Office.

Titled "The American Patriot," the sculpture by artist Lorenzo Ghiglieri measures nearly 4 feet tall. The eagle is depicted carrying an olive branch in one talon and 13 arrows in the other.

It was originally commissioned by Mark Russo, founder and chairman of Foundry Michelangelo, in 2006.

The Presidential Walk of Fame has portraits of past presidents, and Trump's commentary about their legacies was added in December 2025.

White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt told reporters in December 2025 that Trump himself wrote the text displayed on many of the plaques summarizing the former presidents' administrations and their time in the White House.

The president used the display to criticize former President Joe Biden's use of an autopen, displaying a photo of the device instead of his predecessor.

At Trump's request, a bronze statue of George Washington was moved from the Washington Monument to the Rose Garden in October 2025.

The statue is a reproduction of a marble statue displayed in Virginia's state capitol.

The original artist, Jean-Antoine Houdon, visited Washington at his home at Mount Vernon in 1785 to take his measurements and capture a plaster of his face for the piece, according to the Virginia General Assembly.

In March, two more statues of Benjamin Franklin and Alexander Hamilton appeared in the White House Rose Garden.

The White House said that the statues were on loan from a private citizen's collection. The Washington Post identified the donor as Harlan Crow, a billionaire Republican donor and board chair of Crow Holdings.

Trump also placed a statue of Christopher Columbus outside the Eisenhower Executive Office Building near the White House in March.

The statue is a replica of a piece that was displayed in Baltimore's Little Italy and toppled into the Inner Harbor during the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests.

Gifted to the White House by the Italian American Organizations United, the statue's pedestal reads that it was "destroyed" on July 4, 2020, "resurrected" in 2022, and "rededicated by President Donald J. Trump, October 13, 2025."

"In this White House, Christopher Columbus is a hero, and President Trump will ensure he's honored as such for generations to come," the White House said in a statement after its installation.

"Freedom's Charge," a 14-foot-tall statue by Chas Fagan, was added to the Rose Garden in April.

"Freedom's Charge" depicts two Revolutionary War soldiers: a Continental soldier holding a rifle and a Minuteman militia member holding a Battle of Bunker Hill flag, according to Carolina Bronze Sculpture, the foundry where Fagan is the resident artist.

During his first term, Trump appointed Fagan to the US Commission of Fine Arts.

The latest addition to the Rose Garden was a bronze statue of Thomas Jefferson sculpted by George Lundeen, installed in July.

In a statement shared with Business Insider, Lundeen called Jefferson's writing box "the centerpiece of this composition."

"The National Library in Washington, DC, was kind enough to give me photographs and measurements that I needed to make the box authentic," he said. "Designed by Jefferson, this box holds its place in history as the place the Declaration of Independence was written."

The Oval Office has undergone one of the more striking transformations.

Trump added portraits of George Washington, Ronald Reagan, Benjamin Franklin, Franklin D. Roosevelt, and William Henry Harrison to the Oval Office.

He also chose gold urns and baskets dating from the 1800s to display on the mantel, gold medallions for the walls, and gold cherubs from his Mar-a-Lago estate to adorn the doors.

In their book "Regime Change," New York Times reporters Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan wrote that Trump reportedly superglued the gold furnishings onto the fireplace mantel himself.

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

fullText:
WASHINGTON, July 31 (Reuters) - The United States on Friday banned imports from ‌43 more companies over alleged human ‌rights abuses of the Uyghurs, including Hunan Aihua Group, ​one of China's largest capacitor manufacturers, according to a government posting.

The companies were added to the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act Entity List, ‌which restricts the ⁠import of goods tied to what the U.S. has determined are China's ⁠human rights abuses and ongoing genocide in the Xinjiang region.

How many entities are now on the restriction list?

What allegations does the U.S. make against China?

Which companies were added to the banned imports list?

What is the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act?

The latest additions also include companies ​in the ​pharmaceutical, metals, and cotton ​sectors.

Hunan Aihua Group ‌did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The posting marks the first time companies have been added to the list under the Trump administration, and brings the number of entities ‌on the list from ​144 to 187. The Uyghur ​Forced Labor ​Prevention Act was signed into law ‌in December 2021.

The U.S. says ​Chinese authorities ​have established internment camps for Uyghurs and other religious and ethnic minority groups in ​China's western ‌Xinjiang region. Beijing has denied any abuses.

title: Ricketts apologizes after trying to use Capitol Police to block questions
description: Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) on Friday issued an apology for trying to utilize Capitol Police to shield him from a reporter’s questions on Sen. Mitch McConnell’s (R-Ky.) health a day earlier.
fullText:
Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) on Friday issued an apology for trying to utilize Capitol Police to shield him from a reporter's questions on Sen. Mitch McConnell's (R-Ky.) health a day earlier.

Ricketts, in a post online, said he "reacted poorly" and he appreciated TMZ DC's Charlie Cotton for "taking his call" to apologize.

TMZ launched its operation in Washington in April. Founder Harvey Levin said at the time that the bureau would highlight "how politics and pop culture" converge. The outlet uploaded a video to the social platform X on Thursday showing Cotton attempting to ask the Nebraska Republican about McConnell's extended absence from Congress and whether his colleague should do more "to prove his health."

McConnell's office released a photo on Monday showing the senator smiling with his wife, former Transportation Secretary Elaine Chao, at his hospital bedside. He has been absent from the Capitol since June 14, after he was hospitalized for an undisclosed health issue.

Ricketts responded that "we should give Mitch the time to recover," adding that "we are praying for him" before motioning to Capitol Police to block Cotton and another journalist, claiming they were not acting as reporters.

The TMZ reporter pushed back on the suggestion, explaining that he had already gone through security as they came from the basement of the Russell Senate Office Building. Still, law enforcement stopped the pair before the video ended.

The footage has garnered more than 200,000 views, with other journalists coming to Cotton's defense. The video, they argue, was taken in a public hallway where credentialed reporters are allowed to be.

Cotton said he accepted Ricketts's apology, adding that he respects "anyone who can take accountability when they make a mistake." The reporter also noted that he looked forward to his next conversation with the senator.

In a separate post, he added that the "camaraderie of the media here in D.C. has truly been incredible."

title: Bryan Kohberger's choice of 'a house full of women' may hold the key to the Idaho murders' biggest mystery
description: The Netflix docuseries "The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare" explores whether Bryan Kohberger's struggles with women fueled the deadly attack.
fullText:
Bryan Kohberger took the motive for the Idaho murders to his prison cell. One filmmaker believes the answer may lie in why he chose the house he attacked.

"The fact that [this] was the house that he chose. This was a house that had five women living in it. The night that the murders happened, Xana Kernodle's boyfriend, Ethan Chapin, was over, but really, this was a house full of women, and it seems quite clear that he targeted it," Skye Borgman, director of the Netflix docuseries "The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare," told Fox News Digital.

"He watched the house; he was around the house in the days, weeks and months leading up to the murders," Borgman said. "So, it seems pretty likely that he had a very low regard, if not hatred, for women."

Idaho Murders: New Book On Kohberger Reveals Previously Unseen Evidence, Claims Sheath Could Be Inadmissible

"It's all conjecture, but he seemed to struggle with his relationships with women," Borgman explained. "And we look at this incel movement and the question of whether or not he was an incel, and whether or not he didn't like women."

"It seems to me that there was a hatred of women there," Borgman added.

Kohberger, 31, is serving four consecutive life sentences without the possibility of parole after pleading guilty to the 2022 stabbing murders of University of Idaho students Kaylee Goncalves, Ethan Chapin, Xana Kernodle and Madison Mogen at an off-campus rental home in Moscow, Idaho.

Before his arrest, former classmate Lilly Karaban recalled him as someone with a "his way or the highway" attitude who seemed to exist "in his own world."

WATCH: KAYLEE GONCALVES' MOTHER NOT SURPRISED BY KOHBERGER'S CLAIMS OF INNOCENCE, HOPES HE IS SENTENCED TO DEATH

Interviews, court records and accounts featured in the documentary described a series of troubling interactions involving Kohberger.

According to the documentary, classmates described him as "not particularly well liked," saying he frequently spoke down to women, engaged in "mansplaining" and became argumentative or aggressive during interactions. Several students said they found him "creepy" and that he made them feel uncomfortable.

"There were just strange incidents and strange behavior," Moscow Police Chief Anthony Dahlinger said in the documentary.

Former Washington State University Police Chief Gary Jenkins recalled another student's account of feeling cornered by Kohberger during an aggressive encounter. She also believed he occasionally followed her to her car. Kohberger was ultimately terminated from his teaching assistant position.

Jenkins said none of the reported incidents were referred to police because "nothing that occurred rose to the level of a crime."

Ed Jacobson, an FBI special agent involved in the investigation, said in the documentary that "we never saw evidence that shows Bryan Kohberger is part of the incel movement," an online community of mostly men who say they can't find romantic or sexual partners and often direct their frustration toward women.

Follow The Fox True Crime Team On X

"But Bryan Kohberger was very good at hiding his online activity," he noted.

For Borgman, the biggest question surrounding the Idaho murders remains the one Kohberger has never answered: why?

"I would love to, I think, along with the rest of the world, know why he did what he did," she told Fox News Digital. "But it is one of those things that I don't think any of us will ever know. That's a frustrating thing for myself ... and I know especially for the families. They wish so truly that he had been forced through the terms of his plea deal to give us more information about the why of it all."

In the documentary, Karaban said she believed Kohberger "has a thing against women based on the description of what he did to those poor three girls."

"People who brutalize women the way Kohberger did dislike them, find them threatening," she said. "So they take all that anger out on them."

Award-winning author James Patterson, who wrote a book on the case, previously told Fox News Digital his reporting uncovered multiple accounts of Kohberger engaging in unwanted interactions with women before his arrest.

At Seven Sirens Brewing Company in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, Kohberger would push his way into unwanted conversations with female bartenders and patrons. He went as far as asking for their addresses. Some women, according to the book, complained to the brewery's owner about "the creepy guy with the bulging eyes."

"Pretty much everybody we talked to just said, 'This is a strange man with a strange look — couldn't look people in the eye,'" Patterson said. "If he did look you in the eye, sometimes people wished that he hadn't. And his impression of himself was totally out of whack with the way other people perceived him."

In a police report obtained by Fox News Digital, an exotic dancer said a man she now believes was Kohberger visited the club where she worked in 2019, about two hours from his family's Pennsylvania home. She told investigators that while she was performing, the man remarked that he wanted to kill people. When she jokingly asked who, she said he replied, "Whoever I want."

Believing he was trying to get her attention, she alerted bouncers to keep an eye on him. She said the encounter didn't stand out again until she saw Kohberger's photo on television after his arrest and became fairly certain he was the man she had encountered.

Borgman believes Kohberger was trying "to commit the perfect crime."

"He failed in doing that," she said. "But I think his silence is a way of attempting to keep the spotlight focused on him."

GET REAL-TIME UPDATES DIRECTLY ON THE True Crime Hub

Like What You're Reading? Click Here For More

Borgman said police are also "grappling with the why."

"We spoke to one of the FBI agents who worked the case, and he essentially says, 'You've got to be OK with not knowing,'" Borgman said. "And that's really hard for humans to do: be OK with not knowing. And to crawl inside somebody's mind and figure out the whys ... it's impossible. And I think that's one of the reasons people followed this case for so long. ... That question of the why still lingers with just about everybody."

After years of searching for answers, the victims' families are no longer waiting for them, Borgman said. Instead, they're focused on honoring their loved ones' legacies.

"I don't think they expect the perpetrator to talk," she said. " ... The families now are looking forward, not backward. ... Every one of them is committed to trying to help families who may be going through something like this."

"So while I don't want to say they're hopeful, every one of them is taking this tragedy and trying to make something good out of it because that's the only thing they can do," she said. "They can't carry around the hatred in their lives, or else it'll just consume them. So they carry the love forward. And the love is really with Ethan, Maddie, Kaylee and Xana."

Just two days before the documentary premiered on July 29, Kohberger made a dramatic bid to withdraw his guilty plea. He asked a judge to let him stand trial instead, alleging his attorneys pressured him into accepting a plea deal by promising better prison conditions and warning him about life on death row.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

In his request, Kohberger said his attorneys didn't adequately represent him and that his guilty plea wasn't knowingly or voluntarily entered because it "was induced by unkept promises" and threats, The Associated Press reported.

In 2025, Kohberger said he was pleading guilty "freely and voluntarily." In doing so, he agreed to waive his rights to appeal, confirm that he understood the penalties for the crimes and assure the court that he wasn't coerced by his attorneys or anyone else to enter the plea. In exchange, prosecutors agreed not to seek the death penalty.

Borgman said some investigators involved with the case were so shaken by the crime and its impact on Moscow that "they don't work in law enforcement anymore."

"It's something that was too much, and they ended up leaving the police force," she said. "So it's important, I think, to really factor into what happened, the incredible toll it takes on law enforcement and the incredible toll it takes on the community."

"So many people felt fear," she said. "The fear was so deep that they weren't leaving their homes. And that fear, along with the arrest of the perpetrator, also led to this amazing feeling of community. It brought people together."

title: Evans third after roll as Ogier taken to hospital
description: Elfyn Evans holds third place at Rally Finland despite rolling his Toyota on Saturday, as Sebastien Ogier is taken to hospital after crashing out of the lead.
fullText:
Elfyn Evans holds third place at Rally Finland despite rolling his Toyota on Saturday, while Sebastien Ogier was taken to hospital after crashing out of the lead.

Nine-time champion Ogier and co-driver Julien Ingrassia had a big accident on stage 17 - Saturday's penultimate stage - after they ran wide on a fast, right-hand corner and their Toyota crashed into trees.

The stage was stopped and an update from Toyota said both Ogier and Ingrassia got out of the car "unassisted", and were taken to hospital for checks but were "conscious and generally OK".

Sami Pajari, who won his first rally at the previous round in Estonia, inherited first place from Ogier and leads his home event with two stages remaining on Sunday.

The Finnish driver holds an advantage of 46.4 seconds over Toyota team-mate Oliver Solberg, while Evans moved into third place ahead of Hyundai's Adrien Fourmaux after setting the fastest time on Saturday's final stage.

Wales' Evans and co-driver Scott Martin, who lead the standings in search of their first WRC title, were lucky to escape on stage 14 when they ran wide on a corner and their Toyota rolled over three times before getting stuck in a ditch.

Despite extensive damage, they only lost two minutes after being helped out of the ditch by spectators, and team mechanics repaired the GR Yaris at service for the afternoon's four stages.

"I just have to say a huge thanks to the guys for lunchtime, it was a huge effort after my mistake this morning," Evans said after Saturday's final stage.

"And, even more importantly, we're obviously hoping for the best for Seb and Juulien. Obviously they had a big one, so our thoughts are with them and hope that they are recovering well".

Motorsport Ireland's Josh McErlean is in seventh place, just behind Hyundai's Thierry Neuville, but his M-Sport team-mate Martins Sesks was another driver to fall victim of the Finnish roads when he crashed on stage 14.

McErlean finished fourth on the road in for his best WRC finish in Greece, but dropped to sixth with a penalty and a technical issue in Estonia ruined any chance of backing up that result.

Northern Ireland's Jon Armstrong continued on Saturday after an accident on the second stage on Friday but runs well outside the points for M-Sport.

title: From Love Island to Commonwealth gold for McConnell
description: Team Northern Ireland boxer Jon McConnell tells BBC Sport NI of his decision to reject Love Island to pursue his childhood dream of winning Commonwealth gold, which he achieved with a split decision win over Wales' Orlando Holley-Sotomi.
fullText:
A summer spent in the sun on the Spanish island of Mallorca finding love or one spent in gloomy Glasgow getting beat up time after time?

In this unique predicament many would, without hesitation, opt for the former, but Team Northern Ireland boxer Jon McConnell went for the second option.

The 23-year-old turned down the chance to appear on the latest series of Love Island after applying and instead opted to go to the Commonwealth Games.

That decision will have felt vindicated when his hand was raised as the winner of Commonwealth gold in the men's 70kg final via split decision over Wales' Orlando Holley-Sotomi on Saturday.

He's not ruling out a future appearance in the famous villa, although that is put on hold for now as he continues to go from strength to strength in his fledgling boxing career.

"The decision [not to go on Love Island] paid off. If I had have got put out in the first round I might have went 'did I make the right decision?'," he told BBC Sport NI.

"But a gold medal now so they can give me a shout if they want."

Walsh and Rock take silver after final defeats

Boxers choose Commonwealths over Love Island chance

How close he ever really came to appearing on the reality show is a bit of mystery.

He shared a photo on his Instagram story on the morning of Saturday's final showing that on 28 December last year he had marked Saturday, 1 August 2026 as the day he would win Commonwealth gold.

That prediction came true and in impressive fashion.

Holley-Sotomi, who had been "dynamite" on his way to the final according to McConnell, had started well in the gold medal bout, but the NI fighter was unperturbed after a difficult first round.

He changed tact and opted to come roaring back, landing with some big shots of his own.

It culminated in a split decision victory and the fulfilment of a childhood dream.

"I had written that down on 28 December, but that has been a goal since I was eight or nine years of age. I didn't just write it down, I worked for it every day to get to this point and I'm here, Commonwealth Games gold medallist, it's unbelievable," he explained.

"That was a hard, hard fight. He was big, he was strong and he had knocked a few out, but I boxed well. He caught me in the first round and it stung me a bit, woke me up and we changed the tactics, I was busier and stayed away from his backhand.

"It was a close fight, it could have went either way, but I felt I landed the cleaner shots and with a bit of luck, I got there in the end."

The victory brings NI's one and only boxing gold and only their second gold of the Games overall after Kate O'Connor won the heptathlon on Wednesday.

McConnell joked that it was "not bad company" to be in and how he is determined to, like O'Connor, keep striving for further success.

"I was waiting for the right tournament that would put me on the world stage. I was building and building, so it's time to push on for bigger things and we'll see what happens next."

McConnell may have taken the only gold but it was a successful Games for the boxing team as a whole with half of the 12-strong squad taking home a medal.

Michaela Walsh and Kaci Rock also leave Glasgow with a silver while Willie John McCartan, Garyn McAllister and Jude Gallagher, champion four years ago, all claimed bronze.

There was much made of the age profiles of the squad heading over to Glasgow, with eight aged 25 or under and nine competing at their first Games.

While Louis Rooney, Janssen Hill, Eoghan Quinn and JP Hale all fell at the first hurdle, they were the only four to not win at least one bout.

Nicole Clyde and Caitlin Fryers made it to the quarter-final stage while McCartan, McAllister and Gallagher exited at the semi-finals.

Some did receive the luck of the draw, with Walsh, Rock, Walsh, Hill, McAllister and McCartan going straight through to quarter-finals where they were one win away from a medal, but they still had to seize the initiative and push on.

For Walsh, it was a fourth successive medal at the Games, her third silver to add to the two from 2014 and 2018 and the gold from 2022.

She joins bowler Neil Booth, shooter Martin Millar plus Mike Bull and Lady Mary Peters from athletics on four medals at the Games.

Only shooter David Calvert has won more with eight.

She was "speechless" to hear her name mentioned among those greats, but her achievements demonstrate her longevity and she's not finished yet.

"I'm proud of my performances throughout the whole tournament. I have Europeans now in six weeks and I'm using this as a springboard to that and I'm ready to go again," she said.

"[Four medals] It's obviously an amazing achievement. I'm lucky, I love boxing and I'm doing what I love. It's a lifetime of work and it's amazing for the medals to show that."

While Walsh is used to such an occasion, it was easy for younger members of the team to be overawed at a first multi-sport competition, but Rock showed maturity beyond her years, particularly in fighting back to win the semi-final after losing the first round.

For Rock, like McConnell, it's a first major medal at her first Games and she believes it is just the start for her and many of her team-mates.

"I think so many people doubted our team because we're a younger, fresher and inexperienced team but we have six medals coming home.

"We've proven we're only getting started and there's so much more to come."

title: The 'greatest in the world' with an Olympic dream for Team GB
description: Jazz Chisholm Jr's New York Yankees' team-mates tell him regularly just how good he is - but will Team GB get the benefit?
fullText:
He's a Major League Baseball star who could be in line to represent Team GB at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.

And Jazz Chisholm Jr's New York Yankees team-mates tell him regularly just how good he is.

"Sometimes they've seen me dragging a little bit lately," he said in a post-match interview last month. "So they've been saying: 'Let's not forget who you are. You're the greatest in the world... you are Jazz Chisholm.'"

Chisholm exudes a self-confidence that has endeared him to Yankees fans well versed in big personalities and supportive of those who embrace their huge expectations.

Just this week he made headlines for a video in which he was asked to stay silent until he heard the name of a better player than himself.

He didn't say a word - even when the reporter mentioned team-mate Aaron Judge, who is widely regarded as one of the greatest Yankees ever.

But behind the sometimes brash front, there is a humble side to Chisholm.

Born in Nassau - the capital city of the Bahamas - Chisholm was raised mainly by his grandparents.

His maternal grandmother - Patricia Coakley - had been the star player of the nation's softball team. She began teaching her grandson how to hit a baseball from the age of two, and encouraged him to play with swagger and flair.

His paternal grandmother - Judy Chisholm - also played a vital role in keeping his baseball ambitions on track.

When Jazz was 12, he moved to Wichita in Kansas to attend boarding school - the best route to give himself a chance of becoming a professional athlete.

He soon became severely homesick and wanted to go home but Judy convinced him to tough it out.

After graduating and returning to the Bahamas, he was signed by the Arizona Diamondbacks through the international scouting process.

Bahamians are eligible to play for Great Britain in the World Baseball Classic - an international competition that is the closest thing the sport has to a World Cup.

Chisholm was part of the squad for this year's tournament in March - just weeks before the MLB season - and did not disappoint, captaining the team and batting in three runs in an 8-1 defeat of Brazil.

He has made no secret of his desire to represent Britain at the Olympics, but there are several hurdles to overcome.

First, the team have to qualify.

Only one European nation can book their spot in LA when qualifying takes place next year. The competition is open, but GB would probably have to go further than Italy, who unexpectedly beat the USA in reaching the semi-finals of the World Baseball Classic.

Then there are the eligibility criteria. Only athletes who are legally British citizens can compete for Team GB at the Olympics, so Chisholm would have to apply for a British passport.

The final sticking point is the Olympics fall right in the middle of the MLB season, so an agreement still needs to be reached to release players.

An 11-day mid-season break is the latest proposal that may suit all sides as the MLB aims to minimise disruption to its season and the International Olympic Committee looks to ensure it is able to showcase the game's best players.

"I think when you see an Olympic competition, you expect to see best on best," IOC sports director Pierre Ducrey told the BBC.

"That's what we delivered, for example, in ice hockey in Milan-Cortina with the return of the National Hockey League, and we hope we can see that materialising in LA.

"Baseball is a sport proposed by LA28, so they are leading those conversations but we, of course, support as much as we can with the hope that come 2028, we're going to see the best of the best going at it in the Dodgers Stadium."

Watch MLB Bases Covered Live: New York Yankees @ Chicago Cubs

For Chisholm, the Olympics can wait for now - because the immediate goal is to help the Yankees in their quest to secure a 28th World Series title.

The next step on that journey is a three-match series against the Chicago Cubs, with the final game live on the BBC from 19:10 BST on Sunday.

The Yankees haven't won the big prize since 2009, making this their longest run without the title since 1920.

They fell agonisingly short last season - losing to the Los Angeles Dodgers in the deciding game of the seven-game World Series - but are on course to reach the post-season again in 2026.

That gives Chisholm a route to living up to the tag he has been given to his team-mates - help the Yankees secure that long-awaited title.

title: Bournemouth sign Portugal defender Silva
description: Portugal defender Antonio Silva says he is excited to join Bournemouth after signing for the Cherries in a deal worth up to £25.7m.
fullText:
Portugal defender Antonio Silva says he is excited to join Bournemouth after signing for the Cherries in a deal worth up to £25.7m.

The 22-year-old joins from Benfica where he has been a regular since breaking into the first team in 2022 and has featured in the Champions League, Europa League and Club World Cup.

It is a key signing for Bournemouth, who identified replacing Marcos Senesi, following his free-transfer move to Tottenham earlier this month, as a priority.

"I am very happy to be here. It's a pleasure to play for Bournemouth and in the Premier League," Silva told the club's website.

"I can't wait to start the season with my team-mates and I'm excited to be here.

"The mentality is always to win. I will try my best, and I will play for the fans. We have everything here that helps us perform on the pitch, and I can't wait to get started."

Club sources said an agreement was only reached after Benfica's Europa League qualifying-round win over Swiss side St Gallen on Thursday.

The fee for Silva is worth an initial £21.4m, plus a further £4.3m in add-ons.

The defender has 20 caps and was in Portugal's squads for the 2022 World Cup and Euro 2024. However, he was not selected by Roberto Martinez for this summer's tournament.

"Antonio is a player we have admired for a long time and we're delighted to welcome him to AFC Bournemouth," Bournemouth's president of football operations Tiago Pinto said.

"Despite being only 22, he has already built an outstanding level of experience at one of Europe's biggest clubs, playing consistently in domestic, European and international competitions. Those experiences have helped shape him into a defender with real maturity and leadership qualities.

"He is ambitious, has a proven winning mentality and knows what it takes to compete for trophies."

Silva is Bournemouth's second signing of the summer after the arrival of striker Alvaro Rodriguez from Elche in a deal worth up to £25.7m.

The Cherries, who have a new manager in Marco Rose, are aiming for a summer of stability after selling more than £200m worth of players last year.

They are determined to resist offers for three of their key players - Alex Scott, Rayan and Junior Kroupi.

Kroupi is out for three to four months, having sustained an injury in pre-season training.

title: Iceland seizes Paul Watson Foundation's anti-whaling ship and detains its crew
description: Icelandic coast guards and special forces seized a ship operated by a group founded by anti-whaling activist Paul Watson and detained its crew, officials in the Arctic island nation said Saturday.  Th...
fullText:
LONDON (AP) — Icelandic coast guards and special forces seized a ship operated by a group founded by anti-whaling activist Paul Watson and detained its crew, officials in the Arctic island nation said Saturday.

The Icelandic Coast Guard said the crew of whaling ship Hvalur 9 requested assistance on Thursday evening because they believed their safety was under threat from the protest vessel Bandero. It said the Bandero ignored coast guards' instructions to leave Icelandic waters, and later an order to stop its engines.

Coast guards and the police special forces Viking Squad boarded the vessel around midnight on Thursday and detained its crew. Watson was not aboard.

The Captain Paul Watson Foundation confirmed in a statement that the vessel had been seized. It said the 21 crew members were being detained aboard the ship without their phones.

The ship arrived Friday in Reykjavik, Iceland's capital, and police have taken over the investigation, the coast guard agency said. Icelandic national broadcaster RUV reported that police will seek to deport the crew and ban them from returning to Iceland.

Along with Norway and Japan, Iceland is one of the only countries still practicing commercial whaling.

The country sets annual quotas for the fin whales and minke whales fishermen are allowed to hunt in its waters. It exports most of its whale meat to Japan, but demand there has dwindled since Japan left the IWC and resumed commercial whaling in 2019.

The hunt is increasingly contentious in Iceland, where whale meat is now rarely eaten.

Canada-born Watson, 75, is a former head of the Sea Shepherd Conservation Society, whose high seas confrontations with whaling vessels have drawn support from celebrities, featured in the reality television series "Whale Wars" and regularly landed him in jail. He left Sea Shepherd in 2022 to set up his foundation.

Watson was imprisoned in Greenland for five months in 2024 after being arrested on a Japanese warrant over charges of obstructing a whaling ship in 2010. On his release in December 2024, Watson said he would be careful not to be caught again.

"I have to make sure that I don't land in Iceland or another country where Interpol might try to have me arrested again," he said

In 2012, Watson was made the subject of a "red notice" by the international police organization Interpol. He was removed from the most-wanted list in 2025.

His hard-line tactics have split the movement he started, and marine firms have accused the anti-whaling activists of endangering vessels and lives.

Earlier this year, the Bandero collided with an industrial krill trawler in Antarctica in what the ship's Norwegian owner said was a deliberate attack that endangered its crew and could have caused an environmental disaster.

title: Wiebes sprints to Tour de France Femmes stage one win
description: Dutch sprinter Lorena Wiebes takes the Tour de France Femmes opening stage and first yellow jersey.
fullText:
Dutch sprinter Lorena Wiebes held on to a select group over a punchy climb before bolting in the final metres to take the Tour de France Femmes opening stage and first yellow jersey.

Last year's green jersey winner was favourite to win the 85.5-mile out-and-back route from Swiss city Lausanne but was put under serious pressure on a 1.5-mile 4.1% climb just before the finish line.

The 27-year-old Team SD Worx-Protime rider held on to a group of about 20 riders and sprinted away with 200 metres left to win by a bike's length from Mauritius' Kim le Court-Pienaar and Dutch 2023 champion Demi Vollering.

Last year's champion Pauline Ferrand-Prevot, of France, finished in the same group as Wiebes and general classification rival Vollering.

Wiebes' victory was her sixth at the Tour, extending her lead as the rider with the most Tour de France Femmes stage wins since the race's return to the World Tour in 2022.

The two-time European champion is set to wear yellow for only the second time having spent a day in the jersey four years ago.

"I cannot believe it," Wiebes said after her win. "Ferrand-Prevot [Pauline] went to the front and then Demi [Vollering] attacked so I knew I had to follow. It was a long sprint but I'm super-happy with it.

"I'm really happy with the support. The team fully believed in me. Even I had some doubts."

There were two category-three climbs halfway through the stage and both were won from a small breakaway by France's Oceane Mahe who will wear the Queen of the Mountains jersey tomorrow.

Three-time British champion Pfeiffer Georgi, 25, finished 22 seconds off Wiebes in 25th.

The 2026 Tour de France Femmes has 147 riders battling across nine stages - with the event including a first-ever ascent of the famous Mont Ventoux climb on stage seven.

The race stays in Switzerland for Tuesday's stage two which is a 91.9-mile flat route from Aigle to Geneva giving sprinters like Wiebes another chance at a stage win.

title: Leaders Brave extend winning run against Spirit
description: Leaders Southern Brave extend their unbeaten run to five matches against London Spirit while Birmingham Phoenix pick up their first win with a nail-biting seven-wicket victory over Welsh Fire.
fullText:
The Hundred women's competition, Lord's

London Spirit 114-8 (100 balls): De Klerk 38 (28); Molineux 3-7

Southern Brave 115-5 (93 balls): Bouchier 46 (38), De Klerk 2-13, Kapp 2-16

Southern Brave won by five wickets

Leaders Southern Brave extended their unbeaten run to five matches with a five-wicket victory over London Spirit at Lord's.

Captain Sophie Molineux took 3-7 and then added 23 runs in a 52-run partnership with Maia Bouchier as Brave chased their target of 115 with seven balls to spare.

Having put Spirit into bat, Molineux struck early, removing Amy Jones (3) and Marie Kelly (0) within the space of three balls to leave the home side 10-2.

Marizanne Kapp (34) put on partnerships of 27 with opener Grace Harris (16) and Nadine de Klerk (38) but they were the only three Spirit batters to make it into double figures.

Spinners Tilly Corteen-Coleman and Sarah Glenn took two wickets apiece while Molineux returned to bowl Deandra Dottin for five as Spirit closed on 114-8.

Brave lost opener Lizelle Lee for a duck after four balls of their reply while Laura Wolvaardt and Jemimah Rodrigues fell for 13 and 12 respectively.

Bouchier pressed on, hitting a 38-ball 46 from the top of the order as she and Molineux put Brave in sight of victory, only to stumble on the line.

Both batters were dismissed with the scores level, with Bouchier stumped off the bowling of Charlie Dean and Molineux hitting the following delivery from De Klerk to Dottin, before new batter Naomi Dattani hit a winning single off her second ball.

Brave now sit eight points clear of second-placed Trent Rockets having played a game more, while Spirit remain fourth with one win, two defeats and a tie from their four matches.

The Hundred women's competition, Edgbaston

Welsh Fire 144-3 (100 balls): Voll 78 (55); Capsey 2-24

Birmingham Phoenix 145-3 (99 balls): Perry 68 (46), Capsey 51 (29); Voll 1-9

Birmingham Phoenix won by seven wickets

Ellyse Perry and Alice Capsey starred as Birmingham Phoenix picked up their first win of the women's Hundred with a nail-biting seven-wicket victory over Welsh Fire.

Chasing 145 in front of minority shareholder and England midfielder Jude Bellingham at Edgbaston, Capsey, who had earlier picked up two wickets, hit 51 (29) and Perry an unbeaten 68 (46) to help Phoenix home with one ball to spare.

Opener Davina Perrin fell just five balls into Phoenix's chase while Tammy Beaumont couldn't capitalise on being dropped on 10, picking out Heather Graham for 14, before Capsey and Perry came together for a match-changing 86-run third-wicket stand.

Capsey's dismissal, caught cheaply at deep mid-wicket by Graham off the 82nd delivery, nearly proved the turning point, with Phoenix faltering from 24 runs required from 19 balls to needing 12 runs off the final set.

But captain Perry held her nerve, trading singles with Annerie Dercksen before dispatching Graham for a six and a four to see her side over the line.

The victory – only their third in 12 matches since the beginning of the 2025 edition – moves Phoenix off the foot of the table and into fifth place after four matches. Welsh Fire slip down to seventh, with one win and three defeats.

Earlier, the tournament's leading run-scorer Georgia Voll struck a half-century for Fire against her former side, hitting nine fours and two sixes as she top-scored with 78 (55).

The Australian put on 58 for the first wicket with Ella McCaughan and a further 35 with Sophie Devine, who hit a flurry of late boundaries in her unbeaten 35 (19), but Fire were left to rue their lethargic powerplay, posting a run-a-ball 25-0.

Capsey collected 2-24 but Lauren Filer was the pick of the bowlers, conceding just 15 runs from her 20 deliveries.

title: 'Sometimes he wants to leave' - De Zerbi on Richarlison's Spurs future
description: Roberto de Zerbi says Tottenham "don't know" whether Richarlison will stay or leave, as he "sometimes" wants to leave.
fullText:
Roberto de Zerbi says Tottenham "don't know" whether forward Richarlison will stay at the club as he "sometimes" wants to leave.

The Brazil international, 29, scored a last-minute winner as 10-man Spurs beat Chelsea 2-1 in a high-profile friendly in Sydney.

After the match, De Zerbi was asked whether Richarlison - who has entered the final year of his contract - would leave this summer.

"I don't know because I like him as a player and as a guy," De Zerbi said at Accor Stadium. "He's unbelievable in terms of attitude and behaviour. But, in the end, we have to respect what he wants to do."

When pressed on whether Richarlison wants to leave, he added: "I don't know. I didn't understand well because sometimes he says he wants to stay, sometimes he wants to leave. We have to speak anyway. There is not any problem. He's a lovely guy."

The Italian coach was keen to point out Richarlison's professionalism and impact in a chaotic campaign that saw Spurs battle relegation, scoring 12 goals.

"For me, he's still an important player because it's not easy to find another striker like Richarlison," he said. "Richarlison scores goals. He knows the way. With any new striker, we don't know.

"He scored 12 goals last season, not because of luck but because he knows how to score.

"All of us love him, the team-mates, the club and the staff because he works hard every day, seriously every day, and we can't say anything about him on the pitch."

The situation comes in the context of Spurs' record-breaking £237m transfer window, which is set to continue with the pursuit of two more attackers.

One is understood to be Manchester City's Savinho, while Liverpool's Cody Gakpo has also been linked.

title: Root guides Fire to victory over Phoenix
description: Joe Root scores an unbeaten half-century to guide Welsh Fire to a controlled seven-wicket win over bottom side Birmingham Phoenix.
fullText:
The Hundred men's competition, Edgbaston

Birmingham Phoenix 137-9 (100 balls): Clarke 35 (23); Ferguson 2-20, Jansen 2-21

Welsh Fire 138-3 (96 balls): Root 58* (40); Wood 1-21

Welsh Fire won by seven wickets

Joe Root scored an unbeaten half-century to guide Welsh Fire to a controlled seven-wicket win over bottom side Birmingham Phoenix.

In his first match since being reappointed as England's Test captain on Thursday, Root struck each of his first three deliveries for four and top-scored with 58 (40) as Fire chased 138 with four balls to spare.

Root enjoyed a 77-run first-wicket partnership with Phil Salt, who struck four sixes in his 46 (36). Salt survived being caught off the third ball of the innings - bowler Saqib Mahmood was penalised for a front-foot no ball - but had no luck when reviewing his lbw dismissal.

Rachin Ravindra was also out lbw before Jordan Cox was bowled by Mahmood for 20 (14) with Welsh Fire six runs shy of victory. Root fittingly hit the winning runs, reverse-scooping for four before jogging the winning single.

A third win of the summer moves Welsh Fire from fifth to second in the table, trailing Trent Rockets on net run-rate. Birmingham Phoenix have now lost three consecutive matches since winning their opener and remain eighth.

Electing to bat first, Phoenix raced beyond 50 inside the powerplay, Joe Clarke dispatching Sam Cook's final five balls for 20 runs, but saw their innings implode from 53-1 to 79-5, including a dismal spell of three wickets for nine runs.

Cox completed two relay catches on the boundary to account for Mitch Owen and Clarke, who top-scored with 35 (23), while poor decision-making saw Laurie Evans and Rehan Ahmed run out in quick succession.

Donovan Ferreira injected some brief impetus, hitting Ravindra for back-to-back sixes before holing out for 23 (21), with Sean Dickson, Chris Wood and Scott Currie also departing as Phoenix limped to 137-9.

Lockie Ferguson and Marco Jansen finished with two wickets apiece.

title: Mudryk Chelsea return will take time - Alonso
description: Xabi Alonso says he is "very happy" to be welcoming Mykhailo Mudryk back into his Chelsea squad, but it is "too early" to understand what he can do.
fullText:
Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso says he is "very happy" to be welcoming Mykhailo Mudryk back into his squad, but it is "too early" to understand what he can do.

The Ukraine winger, 25, will join Chelsea's pre-season tour after resolving his doping case with the Football Association (FA).

Mudryk has not played a match since November 2024 after being provisionally suspended for returning an "adverse finding" for the banned substance meldonium.

The FA has ended its anti-doping proceedings after Mudryk accepted breaching anti-doping rules and agreed to a suspension equal to the one year and eight months already served.

After a 2-1 defeat by 10-man Tottenham in a friendly in Sydney, Alonso explained Mudryk is joining Chelsea at their next pre-season destination. "Yes, he is coming to Hong Kong, but I haven't spoken to him yet," he said.

Alonso added: "It's too early to tell how he is in terms of fitness, in terms of the game time you need to be involved again, so it's still too early to tell.

"But we are happy for him, especially for him, because we are probably not able to understand what he has been through during this time and how he feels at the moment with the things he has had to cope with."

Mudryk has not been able to train at Chelsea's training ground or work with club staff. Instead, he hired his own private coach and goalkeepers, and conducted training sessions at non-league side Uxbridge.

"We expect that it will take time," Alonso added.

"He trained on his own every day, and I think it had to be really, really hard because he wanted to play football, he wanted to be part of a team, and he was not allowed to do that for such a long time.

"Afterwards we will see if it's quicker or slower, but we need to be aware of that. We want him to feel part of the team. Once he is with us, we will see how things develop."

Alonso also acknowledged Mudryk's return is a surprise, with Chelsea having built a squad full of alternative options on the wing.

They have Pedro Neto, Estevao Willian, Jamie Gittens and Geovany Quenda, while both Cole Palmer and new £117m signing Morgan Rogers can play on the flanks.

"Yeah, to be honest, we were not expecting to have this great news at this moment," he said.

After his side's win at Accor Stadium, Spurs boss Roberto de Zerbi said he still speaks to Mudryk, having been his manager at Shakhtar Donetsk before the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

"He is another who is my son," De Zerbi said. "I am very happy. He deserves to play.

"He is a top guy, a good player. I hope he can show, in this next season, what he suffered over the last two years. Maybe not against Tottenham, but he is a lovely guy and a very, very good player.

"I have to say thank you to all my former players for what they gave me, especially Misha, because I left there because of the war. I left that team, that club, not for football, despite it being maybe the best level of football I have coached."

Alonso added: "Yeah, I remember watching him at Shakhtar, the impact he had, how quick he was, how good he was in one-on-one situations and how he could create a lot of situations on his own. He's a special player, but he will need time, for sure."
