fullText:
Sick of doomscrolling? From venues with smartphone swear jars to cabins with absolutely no signal, here are the fun and freeing ways to ditch your device

There’s a ritual at the start of every event hosted by the Offline Project. Run by Pelé Zachariah, the activities vary – it could be a group walk, a collage‑making class or a supper club – but each one begins in the same way, *with an invitation to hand over your phone. Devices go in a lockbox. Once they’re all in, Zachariah closes the door and turns the key. “I don’t place them in for people, because it’s nice for them to physically put it in the box themselves, walk away, and think: for the next two or three hours, I’m fully present.”

He has been running these screen-free events in London since August 2025. First-timers can be apprehensive about being separated from their phone. “You can sense the vibe when they’re putting it away,” says Zachariah. “People have said to me, ‘I felt really weird’ or ‘I felt super uncomfortable for the first few minutes not having my phone on me.’ Then they’ll say, ‘I didn’t know how much I needed that.’”

Zachariah understands why people might find it difficult at first. “It’s very unnatural. You might put your phone in the living room while you work in the kitchen, but here you’re seeing it locked behind what is essentially a gate that you can’t access,” he says. But when people leave, they often say they would like to have their own phone lockbox, or tell him that they’re going to try to not look at their device until they get home. “It’s kind of sad that we have to literally lock our phones away. But people really crave that time.”

This is true for Jarred Laros, 31, who lives in Essex and has been a regular at the Offline Project since it launched. One of the first events he went to was a “paint and sip” evening, where an artist taught everyone how to paint a landscape scene with mountains, a river and a sunset. People sat around a table together, working on their canvases while having drinks and snacks, and getting to know each other. “I liked the idea of getting off my phone and being more intentional with how I’m spending my time. I would never try to teach myself how to paint, but doing that in a community setting is very easy-going. The conversation flows.”

Laros runs his own business, and spends a lot of time on his devices. “I’m always glued to a screen, whether it’s my iPad, my MacBook, my phone, or all three at the same time,” he says. “Outside of work, there’s the doomscroll that you succumb to. I go on Instagram without intending to. Half an hour later, I’m, like, ‘What am I still doing on this app?’ My average daily screen time is seven and a half hours. My relationship with my phone is not what I want it to be.”

The Offline Project is part of a new wave of digital detox communities that host events to give people time away from screens. It’s not hard to understand the appeal: adults in the UK now spend an average of four and a half hours online a day, and most of that is on their phones, according to Ofcom’s 2025 Online Nation report.

In 2025, the annual TouchPoints survey by the Institute of Practitioners in Advertising found that British adults were spending more time on their phones than watching TV for the first time. The government has recently announced that in spring 2027 it will bring in a social media ban for under-16s, which will include platforms like Instagram, TikTok and YouTube. When the news was announced, a teenage girl went viral when asked by a news reporter how she would spend all her newfound free time. Her answer? “Stare at a wall.”

Thankfully, if you want a break from your phone, there are plenty of things to do that are much more engaging. As our lives are becoming ever-more online, people are starting to push back against the hold that technology has on us. Sick of looking out at a sea of screens, some musicians are enforcing a no phones policy at their gigs. Bob Dylan’s 2025 UK and Ireland tour, Fred Again’s gigs at Alexandra Palace in February, and Harry Styles’s one-off gig in Manchester in March this year all had rules against using phones. It’s happening at comedy events, too – phones were placed in locked pouches at Sarah Silverman’s London Palladium gig last year, and Russell Howard’s current Don’t Tell the Algorithm tour promises “no phones, no distractions, just humans and jokes”.

According to data from Eventbrite, attendance at phone-free events in 2024 to 2025 increased by 121% globally. At broadcaster and DJ Annie Mac’s club night Before Midnight, stickers are placed on phone cameras so you can’t take photos or videos. “It reminds people to be in the moment. You’re only going to get so much satisfaction out of blurred videos with distorted sound, or dark, fuzzy photos,” she says. “Nightclubs are traditionally places where you go to feel a sense of freedom – to be whoever you want to be. They’re meant to be dark for that dual sense of losing yourself and finding yourself at the same time. Phones inhibit both of those things.”

While some are seeking out pockets of time at events and venues where they can escape their smartphones, others are going one step further and ditching them altogether. Cody Ramone, 31, from Derby, was using an old flip phone from 2015 until the pandemic, when life became more online than ever and he needed a smartphone again. In 2024, he switched back to a “dumb phone”. “I got tired of all the notifications and being constantly online,” he says.

Abandoning his smartphone has been transformative and given him time for more enriching activities. “I get bored more. Being bored is what drives you to try new things, pick up an old hobby, or think creatively. My attention span has improved, so I read more and spend more time doing creative hobbies, like crochet. I call people or hang out with them more often,” he says.

What is it that makes our phones so addictive? “Digital media activates the same reward pathway as drugs and alcohol, releasing dopamine, our reward neurotransmitter, in a key area of the reward pathway in the brain,” says Anna Lembke, professor of psychiatry at Stanford University School of Medicine and the author of Dopamine Nation. “Moving images are like catnip for the mammalian brain, leading to video-chaining, akin to ‘chain smoking’. Once we begin, it’s hard to stop, even when we want to.”

The more time we spend on our phones, the more we become “desensitised to what we are seeing” and look for more “potent rewards to recreate that original experience of pleasure”, says Lembke. “At the same time, we lose our ability to take joy in other more modest rewards, like watching a sunset, sharing a meal with friends, or reading a good book. We spend more time scrolling alone. We become increasingly dissatisfied and lonely.”

While that might sound like a bleak state of affairs, the good news is that it doesn’t have to be this way. With the rise of phone-free experiences, it’s possible to detach yourself from your device, even if it’s temporarily. “Part of having a healthier relationship with technology must include discrete periods of time when we are not using it, and instead fully present and interacting with the people and the world around us,” says Lembke. “This means creating collective spaces where we come together device-free.”

From off-grid, tech-free cabins to the pubs where devices aren’t allowed, these are the places to escape your phone in the UK.

Set up in Amsterdam in 2024 by friends Jordy van Bennekom, Valentijn Klok and Ilya Kneppelhout, the Offline Club has 14 chapters in cities across 10 countries, including London and Bristol in the UK. Events start with everyone putting their devices in the “phone hotel”, a lockable metal box with slots. For the first hour, there’s music playing but no talking, and everyone does their own thing. For the second hour, people are encouraged to chat.

The demand for these kinds of events is growing. In London there’s the Switch Off – quiet, phone-free sessions for women where they can journal, collage or read a book – while the Offline Project hosts screen-free walks, talks and workshops. Logging Off Club is a UK initiative – with local groups in London, Bristol, Brighton, Southampton, Cambridge and the New Forest – that has now expanded to Sydney, Mexico City and Winnipeg.

In Bath, friends Nicola MacDonald and Laura Hughes started the Digital Detox Club in early 2025. They host events every two months at The Den cafe in Bath – phones go into the “tech motel” on arrival, and the pair provide optional activities like board games, journalling and crafts. “We’ve been struck by the diversity of attendees, from university students to retirees, which suggests this isn’t a niche concern,” says MacDonald. “It reflects a broader cultural fatigue with constant connectivity.”

If you’re trying to spend less time on your phone, a craft class does some of the work for you by keeping your hands busy. But there are specifically phone‑free classes, too. Native Hands offers basketry, pottery and bushcraft sessions, held outside in an ancient woodland in Sussex. At Curious House in East Sussex, classes range from basket weaving to portrait painting. All sessions start with a mindful breathing exercise to help people switch off.

In November last year, Dan Palmer launched Airplane Mode – a monthly phone-free event at his organic restaurant and natural wine bar, Eat Your Greens, in Leeds. The free events include workshops hosted by local creatives, doing things like painting, collage and origami.

Rather than locking phones away in a safe, they use a swear jar system. “Every time I catch anyone on their phone, I fine them 50p,” Palmer says. “All the fines go to a charity called Positive Action for Refugees and Asylum Seekers. So far, I’ve issued three fines – and one of them was for me! No one wants to be on their phones when they have something more interesting to do.”

The idea of using your hands to make something tangible rather than doomscrolling is what inspired Nadia Butt from Inner Canvas to host art sessions for women at her home in Reading without the distraction of screens. “The screen-free element is at the heart of the sessions,” she says. “We treat it like a ritual. At the start of each session, phones are silenced and placed in a box. I call it the ‘phone spa’. Framing it as something collective removes the anxiety around it.”

Spas are all about relaxing and switching off, but often these spaces aren’t phone-free. That is changing, though, with some spas now enforcing phone bans. The Bath Thermae Spa has a strict no phones policy – guests must put devices in a lockable pouch that’s kept in their locker. At Careys Manor in the New Forest, there’s a digital detox spa break, which includes relaxing treatments, a complimentary journal and a phone amnesty box in the room.

Phones have been banned at the Bothy at Heckfield Place, Hampshire, since it launched in 2023. “Seeing someone on their phone in a space dedicated to restoration felt out of alignment. You are there to be with yourself, to listen inwardly, to slow down,” says the spa operations director, Reka Seres-Erdei.

It’s not just at spas – as sauna culture rapidly grows, many people are finding these spaces offer a welcome break from technology. Ryan Haynes, 34, is a regular at London’s Community Sauna Baths, which has locations in Camberwell, Hackney Wick, Stratford, Walthamstow and Peckham. You can’t take your phone into the sauna, but you’re allowed to take photos outside, although they are considering a phone ban throughout.

Haynes’s Wednesday morning sauna session is “non-negotiable” for him. “All of my best ideas in the past two years have been while sitting in a sauna. Everyone needs to slow down to hear what’s going on in their brain,” he says.

As an independent bookshop owner and a sauna enthusiast, Kelly Wickson had an inspired idea last year: a book club in a sauna. Wickson owns Chapter 34 in Shoreham-by-Sea on the Sussex coast, and hosts the sauna book club once a month at the Nomadic Sauna on Kingston Beach. Creating a phone-free space was a big part of it, and the sauna conveniently ticks that box. “It will ruin your phone; you’ve got no choice,” she says.

The books are always 250 pages or less, and there’s no commitment to go every month. Phones are left in waterproof tubs outside the sauna. The book club is an hour long, and they go in and out of the sauna throughout, with some having a quick dip in the sea during breaks. Wickson has been amazed at how popular it is. “We do it on a Friday evening and it sells out,” she says.

While a book club in a sauna is particularly unusual, people increasingly value being given the time and space to switch off and read. This is the thinking behind Silent Book Club, where one of the mottoes is: “Put down your phone, pick up a book.” It’s a global network with about 2,000 chapters in more than 60 countries, and there are almost 150 in the UK and Ireland.

When Camille Jetzer and James Nasmyth opened the Roses of Elagabalus in Dalston, east London, last year, they knew they wanted to minimise phone use. They refer to it as a “clubhouse” – there’s a bar, restaurant, dancing and cabaret. “The idea of having no phones is that you would walk into the Roses, leave the outside world behind and enter this fantasy world where you can just enjoy the moment,” Jetzer says.

When you arrive at the Roses, a host explains that there’s no photography, and places a sticker over your phone camera. There are also reminders on the menus. “It’s a ‘you were there or you missed it’ situation,” Jetzer says, who has also noticed their regular punters reminding new visitors about the rule.

While phones aren’t locked away, Jetzer says the stickers on cameras mean they are used less. “It creates an environment where phones are less desired. In a dream world, we’d lock away the phones. That’s maybe next year’s project,” she says.

Elsewhere in London, Esmeralda’s Mayfair and the Spy Bar at Raffles London at the OWO both put stickers on phone cameras. In 2019, Samuel Smith’s pubs brought in a rule that customers couldn’t use phones or laptops in their establishments, of which there are more than 200 across the country. At the Barrel at Bude in Cornwall, anyone who breaks its no phones rule has to donate £1, which goes to local charities. In Herne Bay in Kent, the Butchers Arms has been a phone-free zone since it opened in 2005 – there are no signs needed to enforce it, says owner Martyn Hillier. “A disgruntled look from other customers is enough. If that doesn’t work we all start saying, ‘Rhubarb, rhubarb, rhubarb’, louder and louder until they realise they can’t converse any more.”

In Woking, Kim and Mike Jarred run Beyond the Screen, a monthly phone-free social at their local pub the Olive Tree. They set it up in March 2025 after talking about how they could model good phone habits for their teenage sons. They provide activities like puzzles and conversation starters, but mostly people just sit and chat. “Pubs are closing down and we’re just staying in our houses with our phones in front of our faces rather than getting out and meeting people. We’re human beings, and we need to connect with each other. Phones are getting in the way of that,” Kim says.

“Nights out now can feel like content creation exercises. We wanted to remove that layer entirely and return the focus to the room,” says James Hutchins, co-founder of Manchester club Amber’s. It opened in December 2024 and has a no-photo, no‑video policy, with stickers placed over phone cameras. “If people are seen taking photos or videos inside the club, they are politely asked to leave,” Hutchins says.

Amber’s is part of a growing trend in UK clubs, as more venues are making their dancefloors a phone‑free space. The policy is used at both Fold and Fabric in London, Lakota and sister venue Moon Club in Bristol, and Doppler Studio in Leicester. Some clubs ban phones completely. At Offgrid, a monthly day party at House Party in Soho, London, co‑founded by Stormzy, phones are sealed in a locked pouch. At her club night Before Midnight, Annie Mac has noticed a palpable shift in atmosphere – something she experienced during the first phone‑free Before Midnight event at the Warehouse Project in Manchester. “People were more present and louder. They whooped, they hollered, they whistled. They reacted to the tunes in a visceral way.”

In 2019, Hector Hughes was working for a tech startup in London and feeling burnt out. “I ended up at a silent retreat at a Buddhist temple on top of a mountain in the Himalayas. When you got there, they took your phone off you. I spent 10 days cut off from the outside world. It was a revelation,” says Hughes.

He came back from that trip, quit his job and started setting up Unplugged – off-grid cabins in the UK where you lock your phone away. It launched in the summer of 2020; there are now 60 digital detox cabins around the country (and they have expanded to Catalonia, too). The phone-free element is self‑policed, but each cabin has a lock box with a padlock, and the key is in a sealed envelope. They provide a Polaroid camera, a map and an old-school Nokia phone in case of emergencies. Hughes says that Unplugged’s customers often return for regular stays and go on to make changes in their daily lives, like having phone-free date nights or drastically cutting down their screen time.

If you like the idea of escaping to an off-grid cabin and ditching your phone, there are various options around the UK. Unyoked’s cabins run on solar power, have no wifi and often no phone signal – there’s a “spice signal”, from mild to extra spicy, to set expectations for how remote a cabin feels, and how long it might take to walk to one. They also have Brick devices, which help you block certain apps from your phone for a set amount of time. Similarly, Shacks’ cabins are off-grid with no wifi, and lockboxes for phones.

Alternatively, you could look for a remote cottage with no wifi and limited or no phone signal, like the Cottage in the Clouds in the middle of the Lake District national park, or Woodcock Cabin in the Cambrian mountains in Wales. If you want to escape dry land, too, Lilypod in Devon is a floating retreat with three solar-powered eco pods built on a platform next to a lake, where there’s no TV, wifi or phone signal, but there are board games, beanbags and a king-sized bed.

Florence Achery, founder of Yoga Retreats and More, launched her “Retreat like it’s 1999” digital detox breaks, in Lancashire and Cumbria, in 2023. A recent guest enjoyed the break from her devices so much that she forgot to pack her laptop and phone when she left. “I had to WhatsApp the guest she was travelling with to get them to pick up her stuff,” Achery says.

On arrival, guests hand over their devices before spending the next few days sharing meals together, going on long walks, doing yoga and star gazing. “They’re in charge, not their phones,” says Achery, who gives her guests a battery-powered alarm clock to take home, to encourage them to keep phones out of their bedrooms. She has also launched a parent and teen digital detox retreat to help younger people to change their relationship with technology.

At its 223-hectare (550-acre) estate on the River Dart in Devon, the Sharpham Trust hosts retreats focused on mindfulness and connecting to nature; guests are encouraged to switch off their phones.

And, in Suffolk, sisters Lauretta and Sharon Gavin host regular phone-free retreats at the Detox Barn, where guests enjoy vegan food, yoga, sound baths and countryside walks. “For many people it’s a huge relief to step away from their phones for 48 hours,” Lauretta says. “People open up, share stories and properly connect.”

fullText:
Agents withdraw Jerry Falade’s hotly anticipated debut after saying they can no longer authenticate ‘how the manuscript evolved’

A high-profile publishing deal for a debut crime novel has collapsed after doubts emerged over whether artificial intelligence played a role in writing it.

The hotly anticipated manuscript Call Me, I’ll Hide the Body, by Jerry Falade, was withdrawn from sale by its agent despite reportedly receiving an offer for more than $2m (£1.5m) from Minotaur, owned by Macmillan US, as part of a 14-way auction. The plan was to publish it in 2028.

An email sent to publishers by Falade’s agents and seen by the Guardian said: “Jerry Falade produced an incredible manuscript that dazzled us and the top publishing professionals around the world. Unfortunately, we are no longer able to authenticate how the manuscript fully evolved from origin to completion.”

It continued: “During the submission process we vetted the manuscript with Jerry for AI and felt trusting in his reassurance that it was written without utilising AI as a resource in the writing or editorial process. We can no longer substantiate that, and we are withdrawing the book.”

The US auction was run by the author’s agent Marc Gerald of Europa Content, according to the Bookseller. In the UK, Sandy Hodgman of Hodgman Literary is said to have secured several six-figure bids through a similarly competitive process. The Guardian has approached both agents for comment.

Gerald told the Bookseller he first read the book in June, and that it was “stunningly good, everyone fell in love with it. It’s a book that appeals to absolutely everyone.”

He said that halfway through the submissions process, an editor raised concerns that the book had signs of potential AI use. Gerald said Europa opted against using AI-detection software to check the manuscript, saying Falade was “clear and credible” in his explanation.

However, after a meeting on 29 July, when “aspects of [Falade’s] story changed”, the agency decided to cut ties, citing the “need to have total faith”.

“We feel terrible for putting this into the universe and the firestorm it has caused,” Gerald added. “The book itself is genius – however it came to be drafted, it’s amazing.”

Falade’s case is the latest in a string of controversies to hit publishing this year, as authors, agents and publishers grapple with how to handle suspected AI use in manuscripts. Earlier this year, Hachette pulled the US release of Mia Ballard’s horror novel Shy Girl after rumours circulated online that the author had relied on AI, something she denies.

In a statement to the Guardian, Falade rejected claims that he had used AI and said the response reflected racial bias in publishing.

He said: “Three Black authors received major publishing deals this year, and all three later had deals cancelled or disrupted following suspicions about AI. There seems to be a troubling assumption that when a Black writer produces work that attracts significant attention, the work could not possibly be their own. Meanwhile, there are popular white writers who have publicly mentioned using AI for their writing processes and they’re still doing fine.”

Falade did not name other authors, but two Black authors in the US – Ballard and HM Wolfe, author of the viral romance Daggermouth – faced allegations of AI use this year. Wolfe also denies she used AI.

Falade said: “In my case, rumours began circulating and, within six hours, I had been dropped by my agency, deals were paused, and press releases were being issued.” He added that AI-detection tools “are widely known to produce false positives”. He said the novel had “passed through first readers, second readers, editors, and acquisitions teams at numerous publishing houses … If the manuscript had shown genuine signs of being generated by AI, it is difficult to believe that every one of those experienced professionals would have failed to notice.”

title: Courting controversy and befriending Trump - the story of Fifa boss Infantino
description: Gianni Infantino has clashed with unions and European football, but after 10 years as Fifa president he remains in a powerful position.
fullText:
Gianni Infantino has been Fifa president for 10 years, when he was elected with a remit to rescue football's world governing body.

The decade since has been one of reform, expansion and, more recently, controversy.

Infantino was installed with Fifa engulfed by claims of widespread corruption and after predecessor Sepp Blatter had resigned.

Fifa's finances were in a desperate state. There was a reported $550m (£392m) black hole, external after sponsors walked away.

In Infantino, the game felt it had found a safe pair of hands.

"I will work tirelessly to bring football back to Fifa, and Fifa back to football," he said.

Ten years on, there can be no doubt the governing body is in rude health financially. It expects to report record revenues, external of $13bn (£9.6bn) for the three-year cycle through to the end of this year.

But those figures only tell part of the story.

They are boosted by the controversial Club World Cup, and the biggest-ever World Cup with its high ticket prices.

Last month, Infantino and Fifa were widely criticised for the proposal to sell stakes in its competitions - including the World Cup - to private investors, with football's global governing body ultimately scrapping the plan after four days of intense debate.

That led to Uefa declaring it had lost confidence in the Swiss, who has also clashed with players' unions and European football.

This is the story of his presidency and his legacy.

Uefa has 'lost confidence' in Fifa leadership

Infantino on the brink? Who might replace him if he goes?

It is easy to forget Blatter's successor as Fifa president was supposed to be Michel Platini.

But after Platini was drawn into the scandal at the organisation - both he and Blatter were later fully cleared of corruption charges - Infantino was thrust forward as Uefa's preferred candidate.

As the general secretary of European football's governing body, Infantino had been the right-hand man of president Platini for seven years.

But he was an unlikely saviour - a man who was rarely in the consciousness of the average football fan.

To many he was just the guy who presented Champions League draws.

Ten years on, you would be hard pressed to find a football fan who does not recognise him.

Turning Fifa around was no small task.

The US Department of Justice had indicted a large number of top executives and it needed root-and-branch reform.

Two pages of Infantino's manifesto were devoted to more than doubling development money for member associations.

That would be for new competitions, for infrastructure, and even to cover travel costs for smaller nations.

Expanding the World Cup was also included, though to 40 teams. Within a year it had been rubber-stamped as a 48-team tournament.

The election was a close-run thing.

In the first round of votes, Infantino led Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim al-Khalifa - president of the Asian confederation - by 88 votes to 85.

Infantino only moved clear when the 34 votes originally cast for Jordan's Prince Ali bin al-Hussein and French executive Jerome Champagne were reallocated.

The final score was 115 votes to 88.

"This is a new day, a new dawn," said then Football Association chairman Greg Dyke, welcoming Infantino's win. "He is not a politician and he is not an ego."

Infantino, meanwhile, declared he would "restore the image of Fifa".

"It's your money, not the money of the Fifa president," Infantino told delegates. "The money of Fifa has to be used to develop football."

Infantino was true to his word. But to make more money, Fifa had to be creative.

The controversial World Cups of 2018 in Russia and 2022 in Qatar were waiting in Infantino's in-tray.

In his early years as president, Infantino kept a fairly low profile. It was only when the World Cup rolled into Qatar that he started to become a more public figure.

Under pressure amid repeated criticisms about workers' rights and claims of modern slavery in the country, Infantino hit back.

He first called out "hypocrisy" and "racism" about Qatar in the European media, then made his infamous speech about discrimination.

"Today I feel Qatari," he said. "Today I feel Arabic. Today I feel African. Today I feel gay. Today I feel disabled. Today I feel like a migrant worker."

At every game he attended, TV cameras appeared to pick him out in the crowd.

And there was a reason. Reports, which Fifa declined to comment on, suggested television directors were advised that Infantino should be shown at least once each game, but not if he was on his phone., external

Fifa accused of breaching own rules with Trump award

Trump and Infantino - too close for comfort?

Fifa accused of creating 'fake' player unions

After the Qatar World Cup, Infantino made many more headlines - from hosting plans and new tournaments to disparaging remarks about the behaviour of England fans.

Infantino had promised an expanded, summer Club World Cup shortly after his election in 2016.

The plan hit several delays but - two days before the 2022 World Cup final - Fifa eventually announced it would go ahead in 2025, hosted by the United States.

It placed a large-scale tournament in a summer which was usually reserved for player recovery.

Fifa rejected claims players' union' Fifpro and the World Leagues' Association were not consulted.

Then came the unique allocation of the 2030 and 2034 World Cup finals.

It was decided the 2030 edition would be staged across three continents - Africa, Europe and South America. That meant the 2034 event had to go to Asia or Oceania.

With no realistic competition, it effectively guaranteed Saudi Arabia - another country with questions about its human rights record - would host.

Saudi Arabia and Fifa, under Infantino, had developed a close relationship.

Norway's football federation abstained from the process and argued the bidding process undermined "Fifa's reforms for good governance" and challenged "trust in Fifa".

In May 2024, it was revealed Infantino received a 33% pay rise, external - determined by an independent committee - upon his re-election the previous year.

It took his base salary from 1.95m Swiss francs (£1.7m) in 2022 to 2.6m Swiss francs (£2.3m).

On top of that, he was due a bonus of 1.65m Swiss francs (£1.5m), which was unchanged.

Infantino, who was earning about £1.3m when first elected in 2016, is now close to Blatter's final annual salary payment of £2.6m., external

However, a Fifa investigation showed that under Blatter leading executives were being paid huge bonuses running well into the millions., external

In November 2024, with the new-look Club World Cup drawing closer, Fifa unveiled the trophy - engraved with a personal tribute.

"Inspired by the Fifa president Gianni Infantino," it read.

Uefa was growing frustrated with Infantino's profile and his close relationship with US President Donald Trump.

It came to a head in May 2025. Infantino had been on a diplomatic tour of the Middle East with Trump and turned up two hours late for the Fifa Congress.

Uefa accused Infantino of prioritising "private political interests" and staged a walk-out.

Then came last summer's Club World Cup, which was characterised by stadiums with swathes of empty seats.

Yet when Infantino gathered the media at Trump Tower, he declared it to be "already the most successful club competition in the world".

In December, the draw for this summer's World Cup was a long, lavish and outlandish affair.

Infantino was front and centre, and Trump was awarded the controversial Fifa Peace Prize.

Within a week came the announcement of high ticket prices for the finals.

Group-stage tickets are up to three times the price of those for the 2022 World Cup, and the cheapest ticket for the final in New Jersey is £3,119.

After a minor climbdown, Infantino defended the prices and said they reflected the public's "absolutely crazy" demand.

Infantino insisted all the money would go back into the game, saying "without Fifa there would be no football in 150 countries".

He still had one more media mis-step to go before reaching his 10-year anniversary.

In February he had to apologise after saying it was "really special" no British nationals were arrested during the 2022 World Cup.

Infantino came to wider public attention, and attracted further criticism, during this summer's World Cup, which was staged in the USA, Mexico and Canada.

The tournament made headlines before a ball was kicked, with visas to the United States delayed - and even denied - for supporters, coaching staff and officials.

In May, Iran's base for the tournament was moved to Mexico after the US made it clear it did not want to host the team because of political tensions between the two nations.

That was followed by Somali referee Omar Artan, one of 52 officials appointed to work at the tournament, being refused entry when he arrived at Miami International Airport.

Fifa refused to intervene on Artan's behalf, saying it was "not involved in the host country's immigration process".

When the football did begin, Infantino's relationship with Trump was thrust into the spotlight when the US president asked Fifa to review Folarin Balogun's one-match suspension.

US forward Balogun was sent off during the last-32 tie against Bosnia-Herzegovina but was cleared to feature in the next round after an unprecedented intervention from Trump, which drew widespread criticism.

The fallout from the World Cup continued as Fifa opened disciplinary proceedings against Argentina over its behaviour after the final defeat by Spain and throughout the tournament.

The controversial plan to sell stakes in the organisation's major competitions prompted Uefa nations to agree to boycott all future Fifa competitions then led to one of Infantino's senior advisers resigning.

The plans would have allowed Fifa to create a commercial subsidiary to run its main events. External investors would then have been able to buy stakes in the company.

Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said the governing body's own administration had been "deceived" about the project and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham described Infantino as "the wrong man" to lead Fifa.

After a further two major confederations spoke out, Infantino released a statement saying it would no longer proceed with the plans, adding it had become clear the project had "created divisions" that are "no longer in the interest" of its original objective.

Uefa's response was damning - saying it had lost confidence in Infantino's leadership.

Despite the controversies, Infantino has made a clear difference to many football nations around the world. Yes, it is about money. But money for football.

He has enriched some of the poorest and smallest nations, proving funding through infrastructure and development.

And Fifa has been transparent in publishing the salaries of all top executives and keeping funds within football.

After being re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023, he is approaching another election year in 2027.

Infantino will be able to stand again, even though Fifa statutes limit the president to a maximum of three terms.

Only time will tell whether that comes to pass.

A version of this article was first published in February 2026

title: McConnell takes gold as Walsh and Rock claim silver
description: Team Northern Ireland boxer Jon McConnell claims a Commonwealth Games debut gold medal as he beats Wales' Orlando Holley-Sotomi via split decision at the SEC Centre.
fullText:
Team Northern Ireland boxers Michaela Walsh and Kaci Rock both had to settle for Commonwealth Games silver medals as they lost their respective finals by unanimous decision.

Holy Family fighter Walsh, who has earned a medal in each of her four successive Games appearances, has claimed a third silver after also coming second in 2014 and 2018.

But she missed out on the chance to add a second gold to the one she won in Birmingham four years ago after being outclassed by Jaismine.

The decorated 33-year-old also won gold in 2022, and joins bowler Neil Booth, shooter Martin Millar plus Mike Bull and Lady Mary Peters from athletics on four medals.

Only shooter David Calvert has won more medals with eight, four of which were gold.

Three of the five judges scored the fight 29-28 while the other two gave it 30-27 with all in favour of Jaismine.

Walsh made a slow start and had an uphill battle after a cagey first round which she lost 3-2.

The second was a much closer affair and while she went all out for the stoppage in the third, her efforts were in vain as Jaismine did enough to win and claim the gold.

Rock comes away from her first Games with NI's fourth silver after falling short against England's Sacha Hickey.

Hickey just had too much for 23-year-old Rock in an entertaining encounter, with four judges scoring it 30-27 and one 29-28 for the English fighter.

She edged the first two rounds and pushed on in the third to comfortably take victory.

Jon McConnell has the chance to add boxing's first gold of these Games when he fights Wales' Orlando Holley-Sotomi in the men's light-middleweight final at 13:15 BST.

title: Infantino on the brink? Who might replace him if he goes?
description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino is in the eye of a storm after scrapping his attempt to sell stakes in the World Cup. If he goes, who comes in?
fullText:
Life moves fast for Fifa president Gianni Infantino.

It was doing so last month as he was zig-zagging across the United States in a private jet to make him virtually omnipresent as the World Cup reached its crescendo.

On 19 July he must have felt on top of the world as, together with US President Donald Trump, they handed the trophy over to Spain.

Less than two weeks later, Infantino is in a lonely place after scrapping controversial plans to sell off stakes in Fifa competitions to private investment.

Condemned by UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, castigated by fans of the game he professes to want to protect. These can easily be deflected as hazards of the job.

Less so the threatened boycott of Fifa competitions by European governing body Uefa, and its subsequent stunning statement in which it declared it had lost confidence in Infantino's leadership.

Concacaf (North and Central America and the Caribbean) and the AFC (Asia) also - in their own ways - have offered withering assessments of how Fifa is being run under Infantino.

"This issue extends far beyond a single proposal," said the AFC. "Rather, it has exposed fundamental weaknesses in Fifa's consultation and decision-making processes that must now be addressed."

Sources say, in addition to rejecting Infantino's plan, the vast majority of the Concacaf members are either losing faith in the Fifa president's ability to govern the game, or have lost it altogether.

On top of that, Carlos Cordeiro, special adviser to Infantino and appointed by Trump as senior adviser to the White House Task Force on the 2026 World Cup, has resigned.

Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said in a statement to Associated Press that Fifa's own administration was "deceived" about the project.

BBC Sport has approached Fifa for comment.

It feels as though the walls are closing in on Infantino.

But if this is the beginning of the end of his tenure, who takes over?

Uefa has 'lost confidence' in Fifa leadership

Fifa scraps controversial World Cup investment plan

Firstly, it is wise to be realistic.

Speaking to BBC Sport earlier this week, former Football Association chairman David Bernstein said of Infantino: "In a normal organisation, if he has to back down due to something of this magnitude he'd probably be shown the door.

"But Fifa is not a normal organisation. If he has the support of enough of the national associations, he will continue."

Former Fifa vice-president Jim Boyce said he thought Infantino would "still have enough support" to be re-elected but "if things continue at the pace they are continuing, who knows?"

He added: "If I was a betting man, which I'm not, I would still bet he will get his final four-year term."

Infantino has been Fifa president since 2016. Before that he was secretary general of Uefa for seven years. Few know the map of football politics better than him.

Now 56, Infantino became president by beating Asian Football Confederation president Sheikh Salman al-Khalifa by 115 votes to 88. His task was to clean up an organisation tainted by corruption allegations following the resignation of predecessor Sepp Blatter. Blatter was cleared of corruption charges last year.

"I will work tirelessly to bring football back to Fifa and Fifa back to football," said Infantino at the time.

He has twice been re-elected unopposed, and it was expected the same thing would happen again next March. This is not unusual. Blatter was unopposed in 2007 and 2011.

Brazilian Joao Havelange was the last person to unseat a Fifa president in an election, ousting Sir Stanley Rous in 1974. No-one opposed Havelange for five straight terms until he finally resigned in 1998, aged 82.

Letters of support backing Infantino's re-election have been submitted. Will they be withdrawn?

Victor Montagliani (Concacaf president)

Like Infantino, he was elected in 2016 promising governance reform. A former president of Canada Soccer, Montagliani was heavily involved in the build up to, and delivery of the 2026 World Cup, the first to be hosted by three nations. He is fluent in French, Italian and Spanish, as well as English.

Explaining his decision to run for the Concacaf presidency, Montagliani told the BC Business website: "Like anything, when I decide to go, I go. I campaigned on my own dime for three months, went to see all 41 countries, from the US to Bonaire, a little island off Venezuela."

Montagliani took the lead when Concacaf hosted an expanded Copa America in 2024 - in an interview with BBC Sport he rejected the idea it could become a regular occurrence. Politically strong, he smoothed relations around Arsene Wenger's attempt to gain support for a World Cup every two years and has never truly bought into the idea of a 64-team World Cup.

At the Leaders conference in 2025, he outlined why he felt football was strong enough to ride out any storm.

"The game is bigger than world current leaders," he said. "Football will survive regimes. Does it cause a headache? Of course. You have to be realistic about that. That is the beauty of our game, it is bigger than any individual and country."

Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa (AFC president)

Initially elected in 2013, he was elected unopposed for a fourth term to run to 2027.

The Bahraini has presided over significant growth within the Asian confederation, through the Champions League Elite, Champions League Two, the Challenge League and the Women's Champions League, which was launched in 2024-25. The Asian Cup has been expanded to 24 teams.

Sheikh Salman signed off the brutal takedown of how Fifa is being run by Infantino and has carried with him a 46-member confederation, many of whom are aware the figures being offered by Infantino's plan are huge in terms of their overall football expenditure.

Nasser Al-Khelaifi (PSG president and chair of European Football Clubs)

Al-Khelaifi took over as chairman of the European Clubs' Association in the aftermath of the other seismic event that threatened to pull the game apart - the ill-fated European Super League, which collapsed within 48 hours in 2021.

Al-Khelaifi presided over a name change - to European Football Clubs. More importantly, he expanded it to more than 800 members. Of the biggest clubs, only Real Madrid remain outside.

In theory, the Qatari would be a serious challenger to Infantino. But it seems he doesn't want the role.

"He genuinely, genuinely, genuinely doesn't want the job," was the response of a source close to the 52-year-old when asked about the possibility on Thursday.

Mattias Grafstrom (Fifa secretary general)

Appointed in May 2024 and an increasingly influential voice around the Fifa table.

Multi-lingual Grafstrom become Infantino's chief of staff following his election as president in 2016.

Another very visual presence at the World Cup, he could be seen as being too close to Infantino - and the general feeling Fifa's next president needs to be a non-European might also count against him.

Fifa's next president will be confirmed at the organisation's 77th Congress in Morocco next March. Candidates have until 18 November to put their names forward.

title: GB win three golds at European Championships
description: Great Britain win gold medals in the women's four and PR3 mixed coxed four races at the European Rowing Championships, while a men's four development team also claim victory.
fullText:
Great Britain won gold medals in the women's four and PR3 mixed coxed four races at the European Rowing Championships in Italy, while a men's four development team also claimed victory.

Eleanor Brinkhoff, Angharad Broughton, Sarah Marshall and Holly Youd led most of the women's four race before holding off Germany to take their win.

In the PR3 mixed coxed four, Frankie Allen, Charlotte Coburn, Josh O'Brien, Jonty Ridley and cox Omar Al-Miqdadi put in a dominant display as they won by nearly six seconds from Italy.

The men's four crew of Theo Bell, Josh Brangan, Sam Ford and Tom O'Sullivan looked in a strong position and, despite being closed down by Romania in the latter stages, managed to hold on to triumph.

The event in Varese is taking place prior to the 2026 World Championships, which run from 24-30 August in the Netherlands.

The men's team for the Worlds are absent from Italy as they are training in Switzerland.

title: Norrie beaten by Shapovalov in Los Cabos semi-final
description: Cameron Norrie's promising run at the Los Cabos Open in Mexico ends with a three-set semi-final defeat by defending champion Denis Shapovalov.
fullText:
Cameron Norrie's promising run at the Los Cabos Open in Mexico ended with a three-set semi-final defeat by defending champion Denis Shapovalov.

Norrie had returned to some form by reaching the last four - having previously lost six matches in a row - but was beaten 6-3 5-7 6-4 by his fellow left-hander.

The British number two, who won the Los Cabos title in 2021, was broken in his first service game of the match to fall 2-0 down and, despite chances to break back, failed to do so on the way to losing the opening set.

Norrie made a disappointing start to the second set when he struck a couple of stray forehands in the first game before his Canadian opponent broke to love with a stunning forehand return.

Norrie immediately levelled and then carved out two set points on Shapovalov's serve at 6-5 up - taking the second when a forehand volley caught the line.

The third set started disappointingly for Norrie as he was broken in what proved to be a crucial first game.

Shapovalov held his serve throughout the set and completed victory in two hours 39 minutes.

He will play France's Arthur Gea in the final after he beat Hong Kong's Coleman Wong 7-6 (9-7) 6-3 in the other semi-final.

title: Judge orders Waymo to stop overnight charging in Santa Monica
description: Autonomous vehicle giant disturbs residents' sleep.
fullText:
A local judge has ruled that Waymo can no longer use its side-by-side charging facilities overnight in Santa Monica, California, as these may pose a “public nuisance.”

Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Bradley S. Phillips granted this week the City of Santa Monica’s motion for a preliminary injunction in the city’s ongoing public nuisance lawsuit against the autonomous vehicle giant.

City officials and neighbors assert that the constant stream of vehicles at the charging stations create light and sound pollution and cause undue traffic congestion on the streets and nearby alleys, creating a collective bother and disruption.

“The constant ‘beep beep beep’ sound as the autonomous vehicles back out of their spaces (in their own lots) is an incessant disturbance that hinders both our tranquillity during the day and our peace during the night,” wrote Christopher Potter, a man who says he lives right next to the lots.

Under the new order, Waymo is forbidden from operating the charging lots on Broadway at 12th and Euclid Streets between 11 pm and 6 am. The Broadway charging stations sit directly across the street from a private school. Apartment buildings and other residences are also nearby, and some residents have complained consistently for over a year.

With the order in place, neighbors already notice a difference.

“I took a walk around last night, and gosh, it’s amazing,” Dylan Moore told Ars. Moore lives down the block from these Waymo lots and previously created the WaymoProblems.org website. “You can hear the crickets, you can hear your thoughts, it’s not a fleet of locusts descending on the neighborhood, it’s incredible.”

Another neighbor, who wished to remain anonymous for fear of reprisal and described himself as a “night owl,” said that he is thrilled that Waymo has abided by the court order.

“At 2 am when the bars let out, that’s when [they had been] full bore,” he said. “My apartment faces Broadway. The sound of the Waymos, yes, but the acceleration and deceleration sound that EVs have, makes it sounds like you have Tron outside your window. It [was] one after another!”

Santa Monica leadership also trumpeted the success.

“Our residents’ ability to sleep peacefully in their own homes is not negotiable,” Mayor Caroline Torosis said in a statement. “This ruling affirms what our neighbors have been telling us for more than a year, and it delivers relief while the case moves forward.”

Waymo did not immediately respond to questions from Ars Technica.

Waymo began using these facilities in January 2025. After numerous complaints and an online petition, the City of Santa Monica ordered the company to halt overnight operations. It eventually sued Waymo over the issue in November 2025 in a case that is still ongoing. (Waymo has also counter-sued.)

The next court hearing in the case is scheduled for October 2026.

title: Kerr v Wightman for mile gold? Or will Australians spoil home party?
description: The Commonwealth Games men's mile is infused with intrigue and history - and as the event returns in Glasgow it looks set for a compelling final.
fullText:
Josh Kerr and Jake Wightman left the Scotstoun track on Wednesday morning to the sound of The Proclaimers singing about walking 500 miles. On Saturday night, much of the attention will be on 13 men running just one.

The meeting of the two Scots over that mile distance at the Commonwealth Games - just before 21:00 BST - feels like the moment Glasgow 2026 has been building to.

Kerr, the fastest man ever over the distance. And Wightman, who preceded his compatriot as world champion over 1500m four years ago.

Childhood pals from Edinburgh who've been racing in this bit of Glasgow's west end since they were juniors. Bad beatings, grim weather, long car journeys along the M8 with sandwiches for sustenance are in their shared history.

And now they are back at Scotstoun. Different, but the same. Both determined to win gold for Scotland in the historic, reinstated, Blue Riband event of these Games.

But speak to those who know athletics, and they'll take a red pen to that narrative.

They will mention Cam Myers of Australia. Just 20 and enjoying a stellar summer in which he's broken through in the Diamond League. He edged Wightman in their heat on Wednesday in a time almost five seconds fastest than Kerr's.

Kerr and Wightman revel in Wednesday warm-up for mile final

Kerr on why Commonwealth mile glory matters to him

Wightman hopes Scotland can showcase 'ridiculous' talent

That in itself won't trouble the world record holder, who was coasting to such a degree that he had time to conduct the crowd at a couple of points.

But he and Wightman will be wary of the youngster. As they will be of another Australian, Olli Hoare.

The 2022 champion has had quite the time of it, external in Glasgow. First, he apparently stumbled across a murder in the city while on a training run (he didn't). Then it was reported that he was threatened with a blade (he wasn't).

And once he finally got on to the track, Hoare was tripped early in Kerr's heat.

He only secured his place in the final after an appeal, but will be on the start line for the 1609m race and will be a threat.

As will one or two others who might have designs on emulating Cole Hocker, the American who capitalised on Kerr and Jakob Ingebrigtsen's enjoyably spiky pre-occupation with each other to snatch Olympic gold in Paris two years ago.

The fastidious Kerr, it's safe to say, will have kept those receipts. Just as he will the ones from the 2022 Commonwealth final, in which Wightman took bronze while he trailed in last place.

"I genuinely can't wait to watch it. It's going to be a cracker," said BBC Sport pundit Steve Cram, who will be in the stadium on Saturday.

Few know this distance and its vagaries better than the Englishman, who himself is a former mile world record holder and three-time Commonwealth champion.

He praised organisers for the innovative inclusion of the event, which was last run in 1966 and is a tribute to 'The Miracle Mile' run at the 1954 Vancouver Games.

On that occasion, England's Roger Bannister and Australian John Landy competed two months after the former became the first athlete to run a sub-four-minute mile.

And Cram notes the parallels between that and what is to come in Glasgow, just a couple of weeks after Kerr lowered the mile record to three minutes 42.66 seconds.

"It's going to be fascinating," he added. "I don't think any of them are going to completely dominate. I think it's going to be really close.

"I keep saying to people that if I was Josh or Cam Myers, I'd be worried about Jake."

The easy assumption to make is that the Scottish crowd will roar one of their own to victory, but being the home athlete is not neccessarily always advantageous.

You're trying to sort tickets for people right up to race day. You're expected to make time to see friends and family. There are more sponsor demands, more media to do, more people wanting a piece of you.

Take Kerr post-heat on Wednesday. He had already stopped for several interviews before his walk from the stadium to the athletes' area was repeatedly interupted by well-wishers and selfie hunters - all of whom were graciously indulged.

"It's not easy," Cram says. "If it's in Australia, you don't have to worry about whether you stay in the hotel or at home, about how much you engage, how involved you get in things.

"So yeah, there's a lot of extra pressure - if that's the right word - or maybe just distractions when you have a home Games, because everybody wants access to you and the ones who are closest to you can often be the biggest distraction."

Wightman said his plan was to relax in the team hotel and keep his head down between the heat and the final. Kerr has posted Instagram reels of him running around Glasgow.

Neither seem unduly concerned about much other than - to paraphrase The Proclaimers - who's gonna be the man on Saturday night.

title: The four dramatic days that shook Infantino and world football
description: BBC Sport's Simon Stone reflects on the unravelling of Gianni Infantino's plans to sell off stakes in Fifa competitions.
fullText:
Any hope Gianni Infantino might have had of tiptoeing away from the scene of his World Cup private-investment wreckage having sustained only minor damage to his reputation disappeared on Saturday.

Uefa - the governing body of European football - went straight for the head of world game, saying it had "lost confidence" in his leadership.

It was one of the most ferocious statements ever aimed at the holder of that position.

Words such as "shabby" and "secret schemes" spoke for themselves.

It came after a dramatic four days for football that sparked memories of the European Super League debacle of 2021.

The ESL was a splinter league formed by 12 of Europe's biggest clubs, including six from the Premier League.

Former England defender Gary Neville echoed the thoughts of many when he referred to it as "pure greed". It quickly unravelled.

Infantino's private-investment plan did not have a catchy title, and lasted two days longer than the ESL.

But despite football's world governing body confirming the proposal was being withdrawn on Saturday, the infamy will linger much longer.

At the top level, football is a vast, money-making enterprise. The sums players and executives earn is beyond the scope of 'ordinary' fans.

But have we discovered there is a line that cannot be crossed?

Uefa has 'lost confidence' in Infantino's Fifa leadership

Fifa scraps controversial World Cup investment plan

Infantino on the brink? Who might replace him if he goes?

The question many have asked around Infantino's plan is tied into a separate - but critical - aspect of the fundamental reasons behind this week unravelling.

Fifa is a not-for-profit organisation. It has huge financial reserves - over $2bn (£1.48bn) - and is expected to announce record revenues of about $15bn (£11.13bn) in relation to this summer's World Cup.

Given that backdrop - and the reality some countries simply did not need the extra $40m (£29.67m) being offered for football development initiatives if they signed up to Infantino's plan by 19 September - many wondered why private investment was needed in the first place.

It was a question that needed to be asked. But that did not happen in public - or, it has become apparent, privately in Fifa's corridors of power.

Many of Fifa's most senior people - from vice-presidents to special advisers and executives - did not have a chance to ask any questions, simply because they had no clue the plans were being drawn up.

Uefa had strongly opposed the plans from the moment they became public. When they were dropped, its response was damning.

"The current Fifa leadership has not only lost Uefa's confidence but also that of many other members of the football family," it said in a statement.

"When Gianni Infantino asked for the trust and the votes of Fifa's member associations to elect him as their president in 2016, he said: 'Of course we have to be transparent.'

"He told the assembled stakeholders: 'The money of Fifa is your money. It's not the money of the Fifa president. You are the national associations and the money of Fifa has to serve for the development of football and not for anything else.'

"On both these promises, he has failed to deliver."

It was not the first time a lack of transparency had been highlighted.

Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa - president of the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), and one of eight Fifa vice-presidents - referred to it too.

He said any future plans that may impact global football should be presented to members "in a timely, transparent and meaningful manner".

"The future of global football must always be shaped through proper consultation, collective dialogue and respect for the established governance structures of our game," he added.

Football Australia chair Anter Isaac said trust was earned "not simply through good decisions, but through the integrity of the processes that lead to them".

"Football has never stood still, nor should it," he said.

"Some principles, however, should never change. Integrity. Independence. Good governance. Transparency. Meaningful consultation. Due process. These are not constraints on progress."

With the ESL, it was the fans that drew the line - backed by the Premier League, the Football Association and even Prince William.

The plan in 2021 was for the clubs who took part to remain in their national leagues, but also to play each other in a new midweek European competition, which would have rivalled the Champions League.

Critics argued it was a way for the clubs to enrich themselves in a closed league that would have increased commercial and broadcasting income, and the principle of a domestic football pyramid should be protected.

After 72 hours of criticism, the plans all but fell apart. In the aftermath, it was claimed clubs did not get the opportunity to present a rounded case because the outline plan was leaked to the media. That meant the reaction was so fierce any counter-argument would have been lost.

This week has been remarkably similar - except this time, it was people in football who drew the line in the sand.

The only real difference is Fifa did put its counterargument forward in the early hours of Friday - along with an assertion its "planned consultation process was disrupted by incorrect media reports".

As with the ESL, by that point the direction of travel was already established and could not be changed.

With sentiment so strongly against the plans, a damning statement from Fifa's respected chief operating officer Kevin Lamour would have been a crushing blow.

He described the controversial plans as "the project of one person" and claimed Fifa's administration had been "deceived". BBC Sport has approached Fifa for comment.

Lamour acknowledged he had a duty of loyalty to his employer but also to "certain values" and supporting his colleagues.

"Our mission - the mission of the hundreds of passionate, dedicated, and exemplary Fifa employees - is to serve football," he wrote.

"If that means I lose my job, then so be it. I will understand and respect that decision.

"At least I'll sleep well tonight."

Infantino has developed a close relationship with US President Donald Trump, and the pair helped present the World Cup to Spain less than a fortnight ago.

If Infantino was looking for assistance from Trump when he was asked about the proposals for the first time on Friday, he did not get it. Trump said he had not spoken to the 56-year-old about the plans.

A report in the New York Post, which broke the story of the plans being withdrawn, quoted an unnamed source saying the situation had become a "brand nightmare" for Joshua Kushner - brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared.

Kusher founded Thrive Eternal - the American venture capital firm that would have led the proposed investor group had Fifa's plans gone ahead.

As with the ESL, in the end, Infantino was left with no choice but to withdraw the idea.

Now he is left to clear up the mess and build bridges, amid claims support for his re-election as Fifa president in March is receding.

Speaking before Uefa's statement on Saturday, its vice-president Laura McAllister spoke to BBC Radio Four's Today programme.

"All of the confederations will be considering options now," she said.

"There will be moves, I'm sure, to encourage people to stand, but it's early days yet.

"The key thing this week has been to defeat this proposal with unity and consensus and that's what we've been able to do."

Once again, football has shown that while it is prepared to accept many things - and not all of them will be popular - there are some lines that cannot be crossed.

title: Uefa has 'lost confidence' in Infantino's Fifa leadership
description: The governing body of European football says Fifa president Gianni Infantino has "failed to deliver" on promises he made when elected 10 years ago.
fullText:
Uefa says it has lost confidence in Gianni Infantino's Fifa leadership as the fallout from the scrapped controversial investment plan intensifies.

On Saturday, Infantino said Fifa would no longer proceed with the proposal to sell stakes in the governing body's competitions to private investors.

Uefa - which governs European football - had earlier voted to boycott World Cups if the plans went ahead, and other governing bodies also voiced their opposition.

On Saturday, Uefa said it welcomed the decision to withdraw the plan, describing it as "a victory for the whole game".

It also accused Infantino of failing to deliver on promises, quoting a speech he gave when campaigning to become Fifa president in 2016.

The fallout from the plans means Infantino is now under immense pressure as he seeks re-election for a fourth term as president at the Fifa Congress in March.

"The current Fifa leadership has not only lost Uefa's confidence but also that of many other members of the football family," Uefa's statement read.

"When Gianni Infantino asked for the trust and the votes of Fifa's member associations to elect him as their president in 2016, he said: 'Of course we have to be transparent.'

"He told the assembled stakeholders: 'The money of Fifa is your money. It's not the money of the Fifa president. You are the national associations and the money of Fifa has to serve for the development of football and not for anything else.'

"On both these promises, he has failed to deliver. The shabby, back room, opaque deal he hatched and tried to force through were anything but transparent."

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham - who was the first leader of a major country to call on Infantino to resign - said Fifa made "the right decision" to back down.

Fifa scraps controversial World Cup investment plan

Courting controversy and befriending Trump - the story of Fifa boss Infantino

Infantino on the brink? Who might replace him if he goes?

Uefa had been highly critical of the proposals since they were first reported in the media on Tuesday.

In a powerful, lengthy statement released several hours after Fifa announced it had scrapped the plans, Uefa said:

It "cannot keep going on" with "secret schemes of fast-track timescales cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game"

Those responsible for the plan should be identified and held to account

It would devise a plan "with its associations and in close co-operation with other confederations" to make sure this "cannot occur again"

And it would work with partners to "propose a new way of distributing resources through the existing Fifa Forward programme"

It also accused Infantino of "failing to use associations' money for the benefit of the game".

"We must start to use some of that money that is sat idle in Fifa's bank account to deliver the kickstart that the grassroots and the wider game need," the statement added.

"But we don't need to sell off the family silver to pay for it.

"This is a victory for the whole game. But it must not be the end of the story.

"The proposal has gone. The task of rebuilding trust in Fifa has only just begun."

Fifa has yet to respond to Uefa's statement.

The Football Association said it supports Uefa's position, adding: "It is time for a full and robust review of Fifa's leadership and governance to ensure that the global game is run transparently."

Lise Klaveness, president of the Norwegian Football Federation, said it was "reassuring to be part of a strong and united Uefa throughout this process".

"We must acknowledge the entire framework of international football cooperation was unnecessarily put at risk in pursuit of individual interests rather than the best interests of the game," a statement read.

"Going forward, all our efforts must be directed towards improving governance.

"This cannot end as merely another power struggle conducted behind closed doors or through bilateral discussions."

Any hope Infantino might have had of tiptoeing away from the scene of his World Cup private-investment wreckage having sustained only minor damage to his reputation has been obliterated.

Uefa has gone straight for the Fifa president.

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) couched its condemnation of Infantino - and, make no mistake, it is livid - in creative terms.

But Uefa's statement is one of the most ferocious - possibly the most ferocious - ever aimed at the head of world football.

Words such as "shabby" and "secret schemes" speak for themselves.

It is fair to ask why football's powerbrokers didn't step in before now. There have been plenty of instances in the past few months alone when people have felt Fifa's president seemed to be acting against the benefit of the wider game.

But that is a different question.

Uefa has now taken aim at Infantino with a thunderous barrage of criticism, condemnation and vicious questioning.

The damage to Infantino is severe and it doesn't appear anyone is coming to help.

The proposal - first reported in the media on Tuesday - was met with widespread criticism, with Uefa voting on Thursday to boycott World Cups if the plans went ahead.

European football's governing body said the World Cup "cannot be treated as an investment product".

Two other major confederations then spoke out against the plans.

Concacaf, which governs football in North and Central America and the Caribbean - and hosted this summer's World Cup - said its members "rejected" the proposal, with sources saying the vast majority of associations from the region are losing, or have lost, faith in Infantino.

The AFC said it stood in "solidarity" with Uefa and Concacaf, while Burnham said Infantino was "the wrong man" to lead Fifa.

On Friday, Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said the governing body's own administration had been "deceived" about the project.

Carlos Cordeiro - Infantino's senior adviser on global strategy and governance - resigned over the matter, saying the proposal was "a bad deal for football" and would "mortgage football's future".

Fifa and Infantino wanted to create a commercial subsidiary to run its main events, including its World Cups, and external investors would have been able to buy stakes in it.

It said it would "invite third parties to make minority, non-controlling investments" in a new subsidiary - Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE).

In a 25-page document created by investment bank JP Morgan, it was made clear Fifa's tournaments would expand to hit an estimated increased pay-out of 24m euros (£20.5m)per member association in the 2035-2039 cycle.

In the document, the World Cup was described as the "most widely viewed" sporting event but Fifa, by contrast, was said to be "under-monetised".

There was no mention of the women's game.

Fifa said Thrive Eternal was expected to lead the proposed investor group for FFE, had it been approved.

Thrive is an American venture capital firm founded by Joshua Kushner - the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared.

A report in the New York Post, which broke the story of the Fifa plan withdrawal, quoted an unnamed source saying the situation had become a "brand nightmare" for Kushner.

title: Integrate LLM into your Python runtime
description: Integrate LLM into your Python runtime. Contribute to MiskaKan/thinair development by creating an account on GitHub.
fullText:
Probabilistic Python objects. Invent attributes, methods, anything out of thin air; an LLM of your choice (local or hosted) fills in the blanks, with confidence attached.

Code the certain, imagine the rest.

The entire public surface is one class, and the whole idea fits in one line: a Thing is a value with a probability.

The interface is Python itself. There are no prompt strings, no message arrays, and no output parsing: you write ordinary classes, attributes, and method calls, and the model's capabilities are available wherever you left a blank, always priced with a probability.

Everything you write yourself (code, bare values, your own words) is certain: probability 1.0, and the model can never touch it. Everything the model fills in (a field nobody defined, a method nobody wrote) comes back as a Thing that reports how sure it is. The model draws its answers from one axiom: an object is a story, and every interaction is a continuation of it. Everything else follows from it; see SPEC.md for the full spec.

Three operators cover the surface, and only @ <type> costs an inference call:

No class is required. Anything lifts into Thing space: a description in words, a bare value with your own doubt attached, or a whole frozen object (blob @ Car, below). The simplest is words alone, and your own words count as certain until inference touches them:

Requirements chain, and an unmet one drops the value but keeps the probability, so failures explain themselves:

The type operand scales from primitives through schemas to real classes:

You can assert your own doubt, and comparisons happen in Thing space: they are judgments, not byte comparisons:

Subclass Thing and write the parts you are sure of. Written code and bare values are the certain skeleton: they run as ordinary Python, cost nothing, and the model can never touch them. Everything else is imagined on demand:

Provenance is permission: bare values belong to the programmer, Thing values belong to the imagination.

Any method you never wrote is imagined at call time, and it acts: it reads state, writes state (with confidence, journaled), and calls your real methods, which actually execute. Results are Things, so calls chain:

Guard the branches that matter: inside with Thing.require(0.9): any resolution below 0.9 raises Thing.LowConfidence instead of flowing:

There is no chatbot framework, and chat is not a built-in: nobody wrote it, so it is imagined at call time like any other missing method. The object can hold a conversation because a conversation is just more story:

Every turn is journaled, so the car remembers what you said. Objects can also size each other up the same way, by handing Things to a Thing:

car.__getstate__() is a JSON-able document: description, state, story, flags. No code, no weights, no client. blob @ Car restores it with written methods reattached, and pickle works out of the box. __source__ renders any object as the class it currently is:

__story__ is the other lens: the full journal of every event, answer, and imagined step, in order. Consistency and provenance come for free.

Available on PyPI. No dependencies, one file, stdlib only. Point it at any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (defaults target a local server):

Requests ask for the server's JSON output mode (response_format: json_object) and quietly fall back to freeform if the server doesn't support it. Inference climbs a two-tier ladder: questions are first answered single-shot with thinking disabled (and, where the server supports it, decoding constrained to the reply schema); only a question that stumbles (low confidence, a refusal-shaped null, unparseable output) earns the thinking tier. There the stream is supervised as it arrives and cut the moment it starts repeating itself verbatim. A reply the model kept rehearsing inside a loop is harvested as the answer, an answer cut mid-way gets a completion grant sized from the draft rather than the whole budget, and a model that only keeps thinking eventually gets a clear budget error, so runaway generation can never capture the budget.

Or in code: Thing.defaults(model="...", base_url="...", api_key="..."). A URL, a provider object with complete(messages) -> text, or a bare callable all work per instance too: Thing("a car", model=...).

To see what is happening underneath, wrap any block in with Thing.debug(): and every prompt and raw completion is dumped to stderr, labeled by operation (read, imagined, judge, collapse, condense). THINAIR_DEBUG=1 turns it on globally.

An experiment. Every unresolved attribute costs an inference call, and answers are only as good as the model behind them.

title: Hurricanes Make Lizards Evolve Bigger Toe Pads (2020)
description: New study extends previous results limited to just two islands to 188 species of lizard across Caribbean as well as Central and South America
fullText:
Lizards with bigger, grippier toe pads are more likely to survive after their islands are hit by hurricanes. Big toe pads may help the lizards that have them hang on for dear life and survive the high winds of a hurricane. These sticky-toed survivors will then be the ones to successfully reproduce and pass on their genes, giving rise to a new generation of lizards with a vice-like grip, according to a new paper published this week in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

This observation is textbook natural selection, but it suggests that a bout of extreme weather is enough to change the evolutionary fortunes of a species—something many evolutionary biologists had assumed wasn’t possible, reports Nick Carne in Cosmos. Ecologists previously thought that once life returned to normal following the natural disaster, whatever special adaptations might have been temporarily useful amid the catastrophe would fade out.

A circumscribed version of these findings appeared in a 2018 research paper dealing with a single species of anole lizards on the Caribbean islands of Turks and Caicos following Hurricanes Irma and Maria.

“This is a striking case of rapid evolution, which, as we can see here, can proceed exceedingly fast, even within a generation,” Carol Lee, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who was not involved in the research, told Ed Yong of the Atlantic in 2018. “I expect there will be many more cases like this in the future, where catastrophic events impose strong selection on populations, and where populations will need to evolve or go extinct.”

The researchers wanted to follow up on those 2018 results to see if what they saw on Turks and Caicos might be true elsewhere. To find out, the team used photos from natural history collections to measure a lot of lizard feet—some 188 different anole lizard species were assessed.

Next the researchers compared those measurements to seven decades of hurricane data to see if there was any connection between toe pad size and stormy weather.

The team’s earlier finding held up. They found that lizards have larger toe pads in places that have been hit by multiple hurricanes in the last 70 years. This was true across 188 different species of anole scattered across the Caribbean as well as Central and South America. In locales that hurricanes spared, lizards’ toe pads were smaller, reports Joshua Sokol for the New York Times.

If, as climate research suggests, hurricanes become more severe because of climate change, will these lizards’ toes just keep getting bigger and bigger?

“These toe pads are not going to turn into big snowshoes, or something like that. There's a balance,” says Colin Donihue, first author on the paper and evolutionary ecologist at Washington University in St. Louis, in a statement. “Most of the selective pressure is to just be good at being a lizard: to go catch food, find a mate and avoid predators."

A future full of powerful hurricanes may have evolutionary implications for other species as well, Donihue tells Ryan Prior of CNN. “My best guess is that this isn’t just a lizard thing,” says Donihue in a statement. Studies of trees, snails or birds in the Caribbean could be next in line.

“We need more such studies,” Craig Benkman, an ecologist at the University of Wyoming who helped peer review the paper, tells the Times. “And unfortunately, we are likely to be overwhelmed with opportunities in the coming decades.”
